blocks.h: 1. What a bill of lading is, and the law that governs it

blocks.p: A bill of lading is a document issued by or on behalf of the carrier to the shipper on receipt or shipment of goods. Neither Indian nor English law defines it by a single formula; it is defined by what it does, and the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930, section 2(4) reflects this by including a bill of lading within the expression "document of title to goods".

At this sitting the governing Indian framework is the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 (Act 9 of 1856), which deals with the transfer of rights and liabilities under the bill, and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, whose Schedule gives effect to the carriage regime - amended in 1993 so that the Schedule carries the Hague-Visby Rules rather than the original Hague Rules. Article I(b) of those Rules is the gateway: the Rules apply only to contracts of carriage covered by a bill of lading or any similar document of title. The Hamburg Rules 1978 are in force internationally but India is not a party; the Rotterdam Rules 2008 are not in force. Both are therefore worth naming for completeness and must not be applied.

blocks.h: 2. The three functions, and their commercial significance

ul: A receipt for the goods. Article III rule 3 requires the carrier, master or agent, on the shipper's demand, to issue a bill showing (a) the leading marks necessary for identification, (b) either the number of packages or pieces, or the quantity, or weight, and (c) the apparent order and condition of the goods. The proviso matters in practice: no carrier is bound to state marks, number, quantity or weight which he has reasonable ground for suspecting not accurately to represent the goods, or which he has had no reasonable means of checking - which is the basis of the "said to contain" and "shipper's weight and count" reservations.

Evidence of the contract of carriage. The bill is not the contract itself - the contract is normally concluded when the space is booked, before any bill exists. Between carrier and shipper the bill is evidence of the terms; once it passes to a third-party holder its terms become the contract as between carrier and holder.

A document of title. Possession of the bill gives constructive possession of the goods, and an order bill is transferable by endorsement and delivery. This is the function that carries the commerce: it lets goods be sold and resold while at sea, lets a seller on CIF or FOB terms be paid against documents, and lets a bank take the bill as security under a documentary credit.

blocks.p: The evidential force strengthens on transfer. Article III rule 4 makes the bill prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, but proof to the contrary is not admissible once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith - the Visby addition, and the reason a buyer or bank can rely on the document.

blocks.h: 3. The bill issued to the ship, and its counterpart

blocks.p: A bill issued to the ship is one issued by the master, or by an agent signing "for the Master" on the shipowner's behalf - commonly called an owner's bill. Under it the shipowner is the contracting carrier and bears the Article III obligations personally.

Its counterpart is the charterer's bill, signed by or for the charterer, under which the charterer is the carrier and the shipowner is not a party to the contract of carriage at all. The Rules expressly contemplate both: Article I(a) provides that "Carrier" includes the owner or the charterer who enters into a contract of carriage with a shipper, and Article I(b) brings a bill issued under or pursuant to a charterparty within the Rules from the moment at which it regulates the relations between a carrier and a holder - that is, once it is endorsed away from the charterer.

The distinction is not academic. It determines whom the cargo claimant sues, whether the claim lies in contract or only in bailment or tort, and whose P&I cover responds. In practice it is resolved by reading the signature box, any identity of carrier clause and any demise clause. A third document must be kept separate: the house bill issued by a freight forwarder or NVOCC, which is not issued by or for the ship at all and under which the forwarder contracts as carrier.

blocks.h: 4. The other principal types and their purposes

ul: Shipped (on board) against received for shipment. Only the first states that the goods have actually been loaded. Documentary credits normally require an on-board bill, and a received-for-shipment bill is converted by an on-board notation.

Clean against claused or foul. A clean bill carries no clause expressly declaring a defective condition of goods or packaging, under Article III rule 3(c). A claused bill is normally rejected under a letter of credit, which is exactly why shippers press for a clean bill against a letter of indemnity - a practice which is improper where the clausing would have been accurate, because it deceives the third-party holder.

Order, bearer and straight bills. An order bill ("to order" or "to order of X") is negotiable by endorsement; a bearer bill passes by delivery; a straight bill names a consignee and is not negotiable, so it cannot be used to resell the goods in transit.
Through and combined transport (multimodal) bills, covering carriage by more than one carrier or by more than one mode, with the issuer taking responsibility across the legs.

Sea waybill. A receipt and evidence of the contract, but NOT a document of title. It is non-negotiable, delivery is made to the named consignee on proof of identity, and no original need be presented - which is why it suits trades with no resale in transit and short voyages where the cargo outruns the paperwork.

Switch bills - a second set issued in place of the first, usually to conceal the true load port or shipper. Legitimate uses exist but the fraud risk is high and the first set must be surrendered. Stale bills are those tendered too late to be taken up under the credit.

blocks.h: 5. The carrier's obligations under the Rules

blocks.p: Under the Hague-Visby Rules the carrier - whether shipowner or charterer - carries two positive duties and one duty to document.

ul: Article III rule 1 - seaworthiness. The carrier is bound before and at the beginning of the voyage to exercise due diligence to (a) make the ship seaworthy; (b) properly man, equip and supply the ship; and (c) make the holds, refrigerating and cool chambers, and all other parts of the ship in which goods are carried, fit and safe for their reception, carriage and preservation. Two qualifications earn marks: it is a duty of due diligence, not an absolute warranty, and it attaches before and at the beginning of the voyage - it is not a continuing obligation once the voyage has begun.

Article III rule 2 - care of cargo. Subject to Article IV, the carrier shall properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. Seven verbs, and they are worth reproducing exactly.
Article III rule 3 - documentation. Issue the bill on demand, showing the three matters at §2 above.

blocks.p: Two boundaries define the reach of those duties. Article I(e) - "carriage of goods" covers only the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged, the tackle to tackle rule. Article I(c) - "goods" excludes live animals, and cargo which by the contract of carriage is stated as being carried on deck and is so carried; both conditions must be met before deck cargo falls outside the Rules. Against contracting out, Article III rule 8 is absolute: any clause relieving the carrier or the ship from liability for negligence, fault or failure in these duties, or lessening such liability otherwise than as provided in these Rules, shall be null and void and of no effect - and a benefit-of-insurance clause is deemed to be such a clause.

blocks.h: 6. Immunities, the package limitation and the time bar

blocks.p: Against those duties the Rules give the carrier a defined set of protections. The balance between the two is the whole of the Hague-Visby compromise.

ul: Article IV rule 1. No liability for loss from unseaworthiness unless caused by want of due diligence - and the burden of proving due diligence is on the carrier.

Article IV rule 2 - the excepted perils, seventeen in all. Two matter most: (a) act, neglect or default of the master, mariner, pilot or the servants of the carrier in the navigation or in the management of the ship - the nautical fault defence, abolished by the Hamburg Rules and retained here - and (b) fire, unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier. The rest run through perils of the sea, act of God, war, public enemies, arrest or restraint, quarantine, act or omission of the shipper, strikes, riots, saving life or property, inherent vice and wastage, insufficiency of packing or marks, latent defects not discoverable by due diligence, and the catch-all at (q), on which the carrier bears the burden.
Article IV rule 4 - deviation. Deviation in saving or attempting to save life or property at sea, and any reasonable deviation, is not a breach.

Article IV rule 5(a) - package limitation. Unless the nature and value were declared by the shipper before shipment and inserted in the bill, liability is capped at 666.67 units of account per package or unit or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher. The unit of account is the IMF Special Drawing Right.
Article IV rule 5(e) - loss of the limit, where the damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result.

Article III rule 6 - the time bar. Carrier and ship are discharged from all liability whatsoever unless suit is brought within ONE YEAR of delivery or of when the goods should have been delivered; extendable only by agreement made after the cause of action has arisen.

Article IV bis. The defences and limits apply whether the action be founded in contract or in tort, and a servant or agent of the carrier - not an independent contractor - may invoke them. This is the treaty basis of Himalaya protection.

blocks.h: 7. Shipowner, consignee, and the transfer of rights

blocks.p: Where the bill is an owner's bill the shipowner is the carrier and every duty in §5 is his. Where it is a charterer's bill he is not a party to the contract of carriage, but he is not immune: he holds the goods as bailee, and the Rules consistently say "neither the carrier nor the ship" - the vessel herself is exposed, including to arrest in rem. The shipper also owes a duty: under Article III rule 5 he warrants the accuracy of the marks, number, quantity and weight he furnishes and indemnifies the carrier against inaccuracy.
The consignee is brought into the contract by the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856, whose three sections are the whole transfer scheme:

ul: Section 1 - every consignee named in the bill, and every endorsee to whom property passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, has all rights of suit transferred to and vested in him and is subject to the same liabilities as if the contract had been made with himself. Rights and burdens move together.
Section 2 - the right of stoppage in transitu and the shipowner's claim for freight against the original shipper or owner are preserved.

Section 3 - the bill in the hands of a consignee or endorsee for valuable consideration is conclusive evidence of shipment as against the master or other person signing, even if the goods were never shipped - unless the holder had actual notice, or the misstatement was caused by the fraud of the shipper or holder. It bites on the master personally.

blocks.p: In performance the consignee must present an original bill to take delivery, pay freight where payable and give security for any general average contribution. The mirror obligation is the one most often broken: delivery without production of an original bill is at the carrier's own peril, and a letter of indemnity does not change that as against the true holder - it merely gives the carrier someone to sue.

The marks are 3 + 5 + 8 and the weighting is unusually explicit. Limb (a) is worth three marks - a definition and the three functions, and no more; candidates routinely spend a page on it. Limb (b) at five marks wants distinctions with purposes, which is why route step 4 gives each type a purpose in one line rather than a paragraph. Limb (c) carries half the question and asks for three parties and cited law, which is why route steps 5, 6 and 7 are the longest.

The single highest-value habit on limb (c) is to cite the Article and rule number. "The carrier must exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage" is a good sentence; "Article III rule 1" in front of it is a mark.

blocks.h: What "issued to the ship" means, and why the answer says so explicitly

blocks.p: The printed phrase is not a term of art, and part of the examiner's test is whether the candidate recognises what is being contrasted. Limb (c) asks for the obligations of the shipowner, the carrier and the consignee - naming shipowner and carrier separately. That is only meaningful if the two can be different people, which is exactly the owner's bill against charterer's bill distinction. The answer therefore reads "issued to the ship" as the owner's bill - issued by the master or "for the Master" - and says so in terms rather than assuming it.

If in the exam you are unsure, state your reading in one line and answer it. An examiner cannot penalise a clearly stated and reasonable construction; an examiner can penalise an answer that silently answers a different question.

blocks.h: The temporal boundary - and a warning about later material

blocks.p: At March 2024 the Indian statutes are the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 to carry the Hague-Visby Rules. Both were replaced in 2025 - by the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (Act 18 of 2025) and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), both brought into force on 10 September 2025. Anything written about Indian carriage law after that date describes a different statute book.

For a candidate this matters less than it looks, because the 2025 Bills of Lading Act re-enacts rather than reforms: its sections 2, 3 and 4 carry the same three subjects as the 1856 Act - rights under bills of lading to vest in consignee or endorsee, right of stoppage in transit or claims for freight not to be affected, and bill of lading in the hands of consignee conclusive evidence of shipment as against master. The substance you learn does not change; the citation does. For this paper, cite the 1856 Act.

ul: Writing "a bill of lading is the contract of carriage". It is evidence of it. The contract predates the document.
Applying the Hamburg Rules to an Indian carriage. India is not a party. Name them, and the Rotterdam Rules, for status only.
Saying the seaworthiness obligation is absolute. It is due diligence, and it is not continuing - it bites before and at the beginning of the voyage.
Giving the package limitation as one figure. It is 666.67 SDR per package or unit OR 2 SDR per kilogramme, whichever is HIGHER.
Forgetting the one-year time bar. It is the most commercially decisive rule in the whole regime and costs nothing to remember.
Treating a sea waybill as a bill of lading. It is not a document of title.
Answering limb (c) about the carrier only. Three parties were named.
Deck cargo needs BOTH limbs. Article I(c) excludes cargo stated as carried on deck and so carried. Stated but stowed under deck, or on deck without the statement, and the Rules still apply.
Tackle to tackle. Article I(e) - the Rules cover loading to discharge, not the port terminal periods either side.
Article III rule 8. Contracting out downward is void; contracting to increase the carrier's liability is not.
Article III rule 4. Prima facie against the shipper, conclusive against a good-faith third-party transferee. The change on transfer is the point.

Nautical fault. Article IV rule 2(a) protects negligent navigation or management of the ship, not negligent care of the cargo. The line between "management of the ship" and "care of cargo" is the most litigated boundary in the Rules.
Section 3 of the 1856 Act bites on the master personally. A worthwhile point for a Chief Engineer to know about the person signing.
"Name the three functions of a bill of lading." - receipt, evidence of the contract, document of title.
"Cargo is damaged. How long has the receiver got to sue?" - one year, Article III rule 6, extendable only by agreement made after the cause of action arose.
"Your holds were not cleaned and the cargo is contaminated. Which rule?" - Article III rule 1(c), and the carrier must prove due diligence under Article IV rule 1.
"The bosun floods a hold by leaving a valve open. Is that nautical fault?" - it depends whether the act is management of the ship or care of the cargo; Article IV rule 2(a) covers the former only.

"A receiver has lost the bill and wants his cargo. What do you do?" - delivery without an original is at the carrier's peril; refer to the owner and the P&I club, and expect a club-form letter of indemnity, usually bank-countersigned.

"What is the difference between a sea waybill and a straight bill of lading?" - neither is negotiable, but the straight bill is still a document of title requiring presentation, and the waybill is not.
"Who is the carrier under your bill?" - read the signature box and any identity-of-carrier or demise clause.

blocks.p: For limb (a), three words: RECEIPT, EVIDENCE, TITLE. For limb (c), work the Rules as a see-saw: Article III is what the carrier must do, Article IV is what he escapes, and the two hinges between them are Article III rule 8 (cannot contract out downward) and Article III rule 6 (one year, or nothing).
For the numbers: 1 year, 666.67, 2, higher.

ul: Art I(a) carrier includes owner or charterer. I(b) Rules apply where a bill covers the contract. I(c) goods exclude live animals and declared deck cargo. I(e) tackle to tackle.

Art III r.1 due diligence, seaworthy / man, equip, supply / holds fit. r.2 load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for, discharge. r.3 the bill and its three particulars. r.4 prima facie, conclusive on transfer in good faith. r.5 shipper's warranty and indemnity. r.6 one year. r.8 null and void.

Art IV r.1 unseaworthiness and the burden. r.2(a) nautical fault, (b) fire. r.4 deviation. r.5(a) 666.67 / 2, whichever higher. r.5(e) loss of the limit. Art IV bis contract or tort, servants and agents.
Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 - s.1 rights of suit and liabilities pass; s.2 stoppage in transitu and freight preserved; s.3 conclusive evidence against the signer.
Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended 1993 - the vehicle for the Rules. Indian Sale of Goods Act 1930 s.2(4) - document of title.

Why "management of the ship" is the most litigated phrase in the Rules. Article IV rule 2(a) protects negligence in the navigation or management of the ship, but not negligence in the care of the cargo under Article III rule 2. The same act can fall either side: closing a valve to trim the vessel is management of the ship; closing it to protect a particular parcel is care of cargo. Where the purpose is mixed, the courts look at the dominant object of the act.

Why the limitation is expressed two ways. The package basis protects the carrier against a single high-value crate; the weight basis protects the cargo owner in bulk and heavy-lift trades where one "package" could be enormous. Taking whichever is higher means the claimant always gets the more favourable of the two, which is the Visby improvement on the original Hague figure.

Declaring value. Article IV rule 5(a) lets the shipper escape the limit entirely by declaring nature and value before shipment and having it inserted in the bill. It is rarely done, because the carrier prices the additional exposure into the freight.

The time bar is a true extinction, not a limitation period. Article III rule 6 says the carrier and the ship are discharged from all liability whatsoever. It is not merely a procedural bar, and it can only be extended by agreement made after the cause of action has arisen - a routine subject of "time extension" correspondence between P&I clubs and cargo underwriters.

Letters of indemnity in practice. Two situations recur and both are commercially normal and legally exposed: an LOI for a clean bill where clausing would have been accurate (which deceives the third-party holder and is generally unenforceable), and an LOI for delivery without the original bill (enforceable between the parties, but leaving the carrier liable to the true holder). Club forms exist for the second, usually requiring a bank counter-signature; the first is not a club-supported form.

blocks.p: The Hague-Visby Rules were read in an official scheduled text, and every duty, exception, limit and time limit in limb (c) comes from that reading. questions.understand_first: A bill of lading is three things at once, and almost every examinable point follows from which of the three is in play. As a RECEIPT it records what was shipped and in what apparent order and condition. As EVIDENCE OF THE CONTRACT it carries the carriage terms - but it is not the contract, which was made earlier. As a DOCUMENT OF TITLE it lets the goods be sold, financed and delivered against paper while the ship is still at sea, and that is why international trade works at all. Limb (c) then asks who owes what, and the answer is in two places: the Hague-Visby Rules for the carriage obligations, and the Bills of Lading Act 1856 for how those rights and liabilities move to the consignee. retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three functions of a bill of lading?
retrieval_cards.answer: A receipt for the goods, showing leading marks, number or quantity or weight, and apparent order and condition (Article III rule 3); evidence of the contract of carriage - not the contract itself; and a document of title, transferable by endorsement and delivery, included in "document of title to goods" by section 2(4) of the Indian Sale of Goods Act 1930.
retrieval_cards.why: Three marks, three functions. Anything longer is wasted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statutes governed the bill of lading at the March 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 (Act 9 of 1856) and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, the latter amended in 1993 so that its Schedule gives effect to the Hague-Visby Rules. retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an owner's bill and a charterer's bill?
retrieval_cards.answer: An owner's bill is issued by the master or by an agent signing "for the Master", so the shipowner is the contracting carrier. A charterer's bill is signed by or for the charterer, who is then the carrier, and the shipowner is not a party to the contract of carriage. Article I(a) - "Carrier" includes the owner or the charterer who enters into a contract of carriage with a shipper. It decides whom the cargo claimant sues and whose P&I cover responds.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what "issued to the ship" is contrasting, and limb (c) names both parties.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the carrier's two positive duties under Article III.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule 1 - before and at the beginning of the voyage, exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the holds, refrigerating and cool chambers and all other cargo spaces fit and safe for reception, carriage and preservation. Rule 2 - properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods.
retrieval_cards.why: Due diligence, not absolute; and it is not a continuing obligation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the package limitation and the time bar.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article IV rule 5(a) - unless nature and value were declared by the shipper before shipment and inserted in the bill, liability is limited to 666.67 units of account per package or unit, or 2 units of account per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher. Article III rule 6 - carrier and ship are discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year of delivery or of when the goods should have been delivered.
retrieval_cards.why: Two numbers that decide the commercial outcome of almost every cargo claim.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does deck cargo fall outside the Hague-Visby Rules?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article I(c) - only where the cargo is BOTH stated in the contract of carriage as being carried on deck AND is so carried. Both limbs must be satisfied. Live animals are also excluded from "goods".
retrieval_cards.why: Stated but stowed under deck, or on deck without the statement, and the Rules apply.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the Bills of Lading Act 1856 move rights to the consignee?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 1 - the consignee named in the bill, and every endorsee to whom property in the goods passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, has all rights of suit transferred to and vested in him and is subject to the same liabilities as if the contract had been made with himself. Section 2 preserves the right of stoppage in transitu and the claim for freight. Section 3 makes the bill conclusive evidence of shipment against the master or other signer, subject to actual notice and to the shipper's fraud.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) names the consignee, and this is the only statute that brings him in.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a sea waybill and a bill of lading?
retrieval_cards.answer: A sea waybill is a receipt and evidence of the contract but is NOT a document of title. It is non-negotiable, no original need be presented, and delivery is made to the named consignee on proof of identity. It therefore cannot be used to sell the goods in transit or to secure a documentary credit in the same way.
retrieval_cards.why: The waybill is the type most often wrongly described as a kind of bill of lading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A receiver asks for delivery without an original bill. What is the position?
retrieval_cards.answer: Delivery without production of an original bill is at the carrier's own peril. The carrier remains liable to the true holder of the bill, and a letter of indemnity does not change that - it only gives the carrier a claim against the indemnifier afterwards. Refer to owners and the P&I club; the club form is usually bank-countersigned.
retrieval_cards.why: The most common commercial pressure a master faces, and the answer is not "yes".

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changes about the bill's evidential value when it is transferred?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article III rule 4 - the bill is prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, but proof to the contrary is not admissible once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith. Section 3 of the Bills of Lading Act 1856 works to similar effect against the master or other signer.
retrieval_cards.why: The strengthening on transfer is what lets a bank or buyer rely on the document.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can a carrier contract out of the Hague-Visby obligations?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article III rule 8 - any clause, covenant or agreement relieving the carrier or the ship from liability for negligence, fault or failure in the Article III duties, or lessening such liability otherwise than as provided in the Rules, is null and void and of no effect; and a benefit-of-insurance clause in favour of the carrier is deemed to be such a clause. Contracting to increase liability is permitted.
retrieval_cards.why: The one-way nature of the prohibition is the examinable subtlety.

blocks.h: 1. What general average is, and where the law comes from

blocks.p: General average is the oldest rule in maritime commerce: where something is deliberately sacrificed, or extraordinary expense deliberately incurred, to save a venture in peril, the loss is shared by everyone whose property was saved rather than left with the party who happened to bear it.

Two bodies of law say so, and they are different in kind. The Indian Marine Insurance Act, 1963, section 66(1) defines a general average loss as one caused by or directly consequential on a general average act, and states that it includes a general average expenditure as well as a general average sacrifice. Section 66(3) creates the entitlement: the party on whom the loss falls is entitled, subject to the conditions imposed by maritime law, to a rateable contribution from the other parties interested - the general average contribution.

The York-Antwerp Rules are not a convention and not a statute but a contractual code, applying only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them. The current edition is the YAR 2016, adopted by the Comité Maritime International on 5 May 2016; the 1994 and 2004 Rules still govern contracts that name them, so which edition applies is a question of contract, not of date. Where incorporated, the Rule of Interpretation makes them apply to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith.

Contrast particular average, section 64(1): a partial loss caused by a peril insured against which is not a general average loss. It lies where it falls. That distinction - shared against borne alone - is what limb (a) turns on.

blocks.h: 2. The elements of a general average act

blocks.p: Rule A.1 is emphatic in its drafting: there is a general average act "when, and only when" every one of the following is present.

ul: Extraordinary. Ordinary running of the ship, ordinary wear, ordinary consumption of bunkers is not general average. The act must be outside the normal performance of the contract of carriage.
Intentional. A deliberate decision, not the casualty itself. Section 66(2) uses the word voluntarily. Cargo washed overboard is not a jettison.

Reasonable. Both in the decision and in the amount. The Rule Paramount repeats this as an independent override: "In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred."
For the common safety, to preserve from peril. The purpose must be the safety of the whole venture, not of one interest. Section 66(2) says in time of peril.

A common maritime adventure. There must be more than one interest at risk - typically ship, cargo and freight. A ship in ballast on her owner's account cannot declare general average against herself. Rule B extends the idea to vessels towing or pushing one another, provided they are in commercial activity and not in a salvage operation.

blocks.p: Rule A.2 then states the consequence in one line: general average sacrifices and expenditures shall be borne by the different contributing interests on the basis the Rules go on to provide.

blocks.h: 3. What may and may not be allowed

blocks.p: Establishing a general average act does not admit a claim. Four filters apply.

ul: Rule C.1 - directness. Only losses, damages or expenses which are the direct consequence of the act.
Rule C.2 - environment. In no case an allowance for damage to the environment or for the escape or release of pollutant substances. Pollution liability belongs to the pollution regimes.
Rule C.3 - consequential loss. No demurrage, no loss of market, nothing for delay whether on the voyage or afterwards, and no indirect loss whatsoever.
Rule E.1 - proof. The onus is on the party claiming to show the loss is properly allowable.

blocks.p: Three Rules complete the picture. Rule D preserves the right to contribution even where the event was the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to remedies or defences against that party - so unseaworthiness is fought separately and does not halt the adjustment. Rule F allows a substituted expense incurred in place of an allowable one, but only up to the amount of the general average expense avoided. Rule XIX deals with dishonesty: goods loaded without the shipowner's knowledge or wilfully misdescribed are not allowed yet still contribute if saved; goods declared below their real value are allowed on the declared value but contribute on the actual value.

This is the heart of limb (a). The contributing interests are the ship, the cargo and the freight at risk, each contributing in proportion to its value at the end of the adventure. Rule G.1 fixes the moment: adjustment, as regards both loss and contribution, on values at the time and place when and where the common maritime adventure ends. Rule XVII sets the values:

ul: XVII(a)(i) - contribution on the actual net values of the property at the termination of the common maritime adventure, except cargo, taken at its value at the time of discharge from the commercial invoice rendered to the receiver or, failing that, the shipped value.

XVII(a)(ii) - that value includes insurance and freight unless the freight is at others' risk, and deducts damage suffered before or at discharge. It carries the 2016 innovation: any cargo may be excluded from contributing where the adjuster considers the cost of including it disproportionate to its eventual contribution.

XVII(b) - the amount allowed as general average for property sacrificed is added back, so a party whose goods were sacrificed contributes as if they had been saved. Otherwise sacrifice would be rewarded.
XVII(d) - cargo sold short of destination contributes on the actual net proceeds of sale plus any amount allowed.
XVII(e) - mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles do not contribute at all.

blocks.p: Two Rules attach further money to the fund. Rule XX allows the capital loss on goods sold to raise funds for general average disbursements, and the cost of insuring those disbursements. Rule XXI allows interest on expenditure, sacrifices and allowances until three months after the date of issue of the adjustment, at the 12-month ICE LIBOR for the currency of the adjustment plus four percentage points - the 2016 Rules having abolished the old 2% commission in its favour.

blocks.h: 5. Security, the adjustment and the time bar

blocks.p: General average is declared by the shipowner, who appoints an average adjuster. The adjuster is not an arbitrator: the adjuster collects values, applies the Rules and issues the adjustment, stating what each interest owes or is owed. The practical lever is cargo - the carrier withholds delivery until security is given, so the receiver signs an average bond and the cargo underwriter issues an average guarantee behind it; where cargo is uninsured a cash deposit is taken. Rule XXIII(a)(i) confirms their standing by referring expressly to rights to claim under general average bonds and guarantees.

ul: Rule XXII - deposits. Sums are remitted forthwith to the adjuster, held in a special account in the adjuster's name, separate from the adjuster's own funds, in trust. Payments on account or refunds need the adjuster's written certificate and the depositor's approval, or ninety days; all are without prejudice to the ultimate liability of the parties.

Rules E.2 and E.3 - information. Every party supplies particulars of value and gives written notice of any claim as soon as possible. After twelve months the adjuster may estimate, and an estimate is challengeable only within two months and only as manifestly incorrect.

Rule XXIII - time bar. Rights to contribution, including under bonds and guarantees, are extinguished unless action is brought within one year of issue of the adjustment, and never more than six years from termination of the adventure. Extendable by agreement; inapplicable between the parties and their own insurers.

blocks.h: 6. Scenarios in which general average is declared

blocks.p: The numbered Rules are, in effect, the examiner's list of examples. Each is a decided category, and quoting the Rule number turns a story into a legal answer.

ul: Jettison of cargo (Rule I) - allowed only if that cargo was carried in accordance with the recognised custom of the trade.
Sacrifice for the common safety (Rule II) - including water going down hatches opened to make a jettison, so cargo never itself sacrificed is still allowed.
Extinguishing fire (Rule III) - water and other fire-fighting damage, including beaching or scuttling a burning ship; but no allowance for damage by smoke however caused, or by heat of the fire.
Voluntary stranding (Rule V) - a ship intentionally run ashore for the common safety, whether or not she might have been driven ashore anyway.

Machinery and boiler damage refloating (Rule VII) - allowed where the ship is ashore and in a position of peril and the damage arose from an actual intention to float her for the common safety at the risk of such damage. Where she is afloat, no such damage is allowed in any circumstances.
Lightening a ship when ashore (Rule VIII) - the extra cost of lightening, lighter hire and reshipping, and consequent damage.
Cargo, materials or stores burnt as fuel (Rule IX) - with credit to general average for the fuel that would otherwise have been consumed.

Port of refuge (Rules X and XI) - entry and departure expenses where the ship put in in consequence of accident, sacrifice or other extraordinary circumstances necessary for the common safety; plus handling, discharging, storage and reloading, and the wages and maintenance of master, officers and crew during the detention.

Salvage remuneration (Rule VI) - allowable where the operation preserved the property from peril; where the parties are separately liable to salvors it is allowed only if one of five conditions applies, and Rule VI(d) excludes article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC altogether.
And the counter-example, Rule IV - cutting away wreck already carried away or effectively lost by accident is not general average. There is nothing left to sacrifice.

blocks.h: 7. Criteria and conditions in modern maritime commerce

blocks.p: Set against any scenario, six conditions decide whether general average applies.

ul: Real peril - real and substantial, though not necessarily immediate. A precaution in fine weather is not general average.
A common adventure - two or more interests must stand to lose. This is why the question says "among parties involved in a maritime venture".
A voluntary act - the casualty is the peril; the response is the act.
Extraordinary and reasonable - separate gates, with the Rule Paramount making reasonableness an override on every allowance.
Success, a saved fund - contribution is levied on values at the end of the adventure (Rules G.1 and XVII). If nothing survives there is nothing to contribute from.
Incorporation - the Rules bind only because the contract of carriage says so; absent that, the position falls back on the general maritime law and, in India, the Marine Insurance Act 1963.

blocks.p: Modern commerce has changed the economics rather than the principle, and the 2016 Rules answer that directly. Containerisation means one casualty can involve thousands of consignees, making security collection disproportionate to the sums recovered - which is why Rule XVII(a)(ii) now lets the adjuster exclude low-value cargo and why Rule E.3 imposes a twelve-month cut-off backed by a power to estimate. Rule C.2 keeps the pollution regimes out of the adjustment, and Rule VI(b) stops salvage being adjusted twice where salvors have been paid separately.

The printed marks are 8 + 8, and the trap is that limb (a) names three things: the concept, the principles, and contribution among the parties. Most candidates write four hundred words on "what is general average" and then run out of time before contribution - which is the part the examiner has singled out and which no textbook paragraph covers. Route steps 1 to 3 handle the concept and principles briskly; steps 4 and 5 spend the marks where the question points.

Limb (b) asks for two things at once - examples and criteria and conditions. Splitting them into steps 6 and 7 means neither is dropped. Step 6 is a list of Rules; step 7 is the reasoning that governs all of them.

blocks.h: Statute, contract, convention - keep the three apart

blocks.p: General average is unusual in that the instrument students quote most - the York-Antwerp Rules - has no legislative force at all. It is a set of contractual terms produced by a private international body, the CMI, and binds only where a bill of lading or charterparty incorporates it. The Marine Insurance Act 1963 is the Indian statute, and it governs the insurance relationship - what the assured may recover from the underwriter - as much as the adjustment itself.

This matters practically. If asked "which York-Antwerp Rules apply to this casualty?", the answer is whichever edition the contract names. A 2024 casualty under a bill of lading referring to the YAR 1994 is adjusted on the 1994 Rules. Saying "the 2016 Rules, because they are the latest" is wrong.

blocks.h: What changed in 2016, and why it is worth knowing

ul: Rule VI (salvage). The 2004 Rules had removed salvage from general average and were consequently almost never used. The 2016 Rules restore it, subject to the five gateways at VI(b) which prevent pointless re-adjustment where salvors have been paid separately.

Rules X, XI and XIV. The 1994 wording for port of refuge expenses, crew wages and temporary repairs was retained - the main reason shipowners accepted the 2016 Rules where they had rejected the 2004 Rules.
Rule XVII. The low-value cargo exclusion is new, and is the clearest example of the Rules bending to container economics.
Rules XX and XXI. The old 2% commission on general average disbursements was abolished, replaced by interest at 12-month ICE LIBOR + 4 percentage points.

blocks.p: BIMCO agreed in May 2016 that its charterparties and bills of lading should refer to the 2016 Rules, which is how the edition spread into standard forms.

ul: Writing the history of the Rhodian law and Lex Mercatoria. It earns nothing. The examiner asked for principles and contribution.
Answering limb (a) without ever reaching contribution. Half the limb is about who pays what.
Saying general average is "a convention" or "IMO law". It is neither.
Forgetting that sacrificed property still contributes (Rule XVII(b)). Candidates routinely say the jettisoned cargo owner "is paid and contributes nothing".
Treating fire damage as wholly allowable. Smoke and heat damage are excluded by Rule III - they are the peril, not the sacrifice.
Claiming machinery damage in general average for a ship that is afloat. Rule VII excludes it in any circumstances.
Saying fault defeats general average. Rule D says the opposite - the adjustment proceeds and fault is fought separately.
"Only when". Rule A.1 uses those words. Every element must be present; the examiner is testing whether you know it is a conjunctive test.
Voluntary versus accidental. Cargo washed overboard is a particular average loss; cargo jettisoned is general average. Same cargo, same sea.
Rule IV. Cutting away a mast already carried away is not a sacrifice - a favourite oral question.
Rule XVII(e). Mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles do not contribute. Easy marks, rarely given.
The two time limits. Rule E.3's twelve months for particulars of value is not the same thing as Rule XXIII's one year from the adjustment, six years absolute.
SCOPIC. Rule VI(d) puts article 14 special compensation and SCOPIC outside general average.

"Your ship grounds and you damage the main engine trying to refloat. Is that general average?" - Rule VII: yes if she was ashore and in peril and the damage arose from an actual intention to refloat for the common safety; no if she was afloat.
"Who declares general average, and who pays the adjuster?" - the shipowner declares and appoints; the adjuster's fee is a general average disbursement borne by the fund.
"What is the difference between an average bond and an average guarantee?" - the bond is given by the cargo receiver, the guarantee by the cargo underwriter backing it.
"Can you refuse to deliver cargo until security is given?" - yes, that is the practical basis on which security is collected.
"The grounding was caused by our own negligent navigation. Can we still claim?" - Rule D: rights to contribution are unaffected, without prejudice to defences against us.
"Give three items that do not contribute." - Rule XVII(e).
"What is a substituted expense?" - Rule F, capped at the general average expense avoided; towage to destination in place of repairs at a port of refuge is the standard illustration.

blocks.p: For the elements, hold five words in Rule A order: EXTRAORDINARY, INTENTIONAL, REASONABLE, COMMON SAFETY, COMMON ADVENTURE - then add SAVED, because contribution is levied on what survives. Six gates, and every scenario in limb (b) is tested against them.

For contribution, remember the sequence VALUE - ADD BACK - EXCLUDE - APPORTION: take the actual net value at the end of the adventure (Rule XVII(a)); add back what was sacrificed (XVII(b)); exclude what does not contribute (XVII(e), and uneconomic cargo under XVII(a)(ii)); apportion the fund rateably (s.66(3), Rule A.2).

blocks.h: The scenarios in longer form - detail behind route step 6

blocks.p: The Model Answer states each category as a proposition plus its Rule number, which is what scores. The colour below is for the oral and for reading around the topic.

ul: Jettison. The custom-of-the-trade condition in Rule I is aimed squarely at deck cargo. Containers stowed on deck under a modern trade where deck carriage is customary are within the Rule; goods stowed on deck against the custom of that trade are not, and their jettison earns no allowance.

Fire. Rule III draws the sharpest line in the Rules between peril damage and sacrifice damage. The water you put on the fire is a sacrifice; the smoke and the heat are the casualty. Beaching or scuttling a burning ship is expressly on the sacrifice side, which is why a deliberate flooding decision is worth recording carefully in the engine room log and the deck log alike.

Refloating. Rule VII is the one a Chief Engineer meets in practice. Working the main engine hard astern with the ship aground, knowing the risk to bearings, tailshaft, boilers or coolers, is a classic general average sacrifice - provided the ship was in a position of peril and the intention is evidenced. The engine-room record of the order, the times, the loads and the reason is what proves that intention months later, and its absence is the usual reason such a claim fails.

Port of refuge. This is the largest single head of general average expenditure in practice, because Rules X and XI between them pick up entry, discharge, storage, reloading, departure, and crew wages and maintenance for the whole detention. Rule X(a)(ii) extends the same treatment to a second port where repairs cannot be done at the first, including temporary repairs and towage.

Salvage. The five gateways at Rule VI(b) exist because, where every interest has already settled with the salvors under its own Lloyd's Open Form apportionment, putting salvage back through the general average adjustment usually moves very little money and costs a great deal. The gateways admit it only where it makes a real difference - for example where there are significant general average sacrifices, or where salved values are manifestly incorrect.

The Marine Insurance Act 1963 was read from a complete third-party reproduction of the Act, because India Code refuses automated retrieval. questions.understand_first: General average is a loss-sharing rule, not an insurance product and not a safety regulation. One party deliberately gives something up so that everyone's property survives; the law then makes everyone whose property survived pay a share. Two sources say so, and they are different in kind: the Marine Insurance Act 1963 is Indian statute, and the York-Antwerp Rules are a contractual code that binds only because the bill of lading incorporates it. The examiner has asked for THREE things in limb (a) - the concept, the principles, and contribution among the parties - and contribution is the one candidates never reach. Limb (b) then asks you to test concrete scenarios against the criteria, which is exactly what the numbered Rules do.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a general average act in the words of Rule A.1.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: "When, and only when" signals a conjunctive test - every element must be present.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act 1963 provide?
retrieval_cards.answer: s.66(1) a general average loss is caused by or directly consequential on a general average act and includes expenditure as well as sacrifice; s.66(2) the act is an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure voluntarily and reasonably made in time of peril to preserve the property imperilled in the common adventure; s.66(3) the party on whom it falls is entitled to a rateable contribution from the other parties interested.
retrieval_cards.why: The statutory limb of the answer - the York-Antwerp Rules are not legislation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are the York-Antwerp Rules not a convention, and what follows from that?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are a private contractual code produced by the CMI. They bind only where the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, so which edition applies - 1994, 2004 or 2016 - is decided by the contract, not by the date of the casualty. Where incorporated, the Rule of Interpretation makes them apply to the exclusion of any inconsistent law and practice.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common error is to assert the latest edition applies automatically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what basis is the contribution calculated?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule G.1 - on values at the time and place where the common maritime adventure ends. Rule XVII(a)(i) - actual net values of the property at termination, except cargo, taken at its value at time of discharge from the commercial invoice to the receiver or the shipped value. Rule XVII(b) - the amount allowed as general average for property sacrificed is added back, so sacrificed property still contributes.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the "contribution among parties" the question names expressly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which interests do not contribute to general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule XVII(e) - mails, passengers' luggage, accompanied personal effects and accompanied private motor vehicles. Separately, under Rule XVII(a)(ii) the adjuster may exclude any cargo where the cost of including it would be disproportionate to its eventual contribution.
retrieval_cards.why: Four exact categories, plus the 2016 discretionary exclusion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the shipowner's own negligent navigation. Does general average still apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, but this is without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against that party. The adjustment proceeds; fault is litigated separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely say fault destroys the claim. It does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You damage the main engine trying to refloat. When is that general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule VII - damage to machinery and boilers is allowed when the ship is ashore and in a position of peril and the damage is shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float her for the common safety at the risk of such damage. Where the ship is afloat, no loss or damage from working the propelling machinery and boilers is allowed in any circumstances.
retrieval_cards.why: The engineering scenario most likely to be put to a Chief Engineer orally.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an average bond and an average guarantee?
retrieval_cards.answer: The average bond is given by the cargo receiver, undertaking to pay the contribution once adjusted and to supply the values the adjuster needs. The average guarantee is given by the cargo underwriter to back that undertaking. Where cargo is uninsured a cash deposit is taken instead, and Rule XXII requires it to be held in a special account in the adjuster's name, separate from the adjuster's own funds.
retrieval_cards.why: Security is how the contribution is actually collected before cargo is released.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the general average time bar.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule XXIII(a)(i) - rights to contribution, including under general average bonds and guarantees, are extinguished unless action is brought within one year after the date the adjustment is issued, and in no case more than six years from termination of the common maritime adventure. Extendable by agreement, and not applicable between the parties and their own insurers.
retrieval_cards.why: Two limits, and they are commonly confused with Rule E.3's twelve months.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Fire on board. Which fire damage is general average and which is not?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule III - damage done to ship and cargo by water or otherwise in extinguishing the fire, including damage by beaching or scuttling a burning ship, is allowed. But no allowance is made for damage by smoke however caused, or by heat of the fire - that is damage by the peril, not by the sacrifice.
retrieval_cards.why: The clearest illustration of the sacrifice-versus-peril line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a substituted expense?
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule F - any additional expense incurred in place of another expense which would have been allowable as general average is deemed to be general average and allowed without regard to any saving to other interests, but only up to the amount of the general average expense avoided.
retrieval_cards.why: The cap is the examinable part, and it is routinely omitted.

blocks.h: 1. The instrument, and which revision applies

blocks.p: The question names MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3. The circular was approved jointly by the Facilitation Committee at its 41st session (4 to 7 April 2017) and the Maritime Safety Committee at its 98th session (7 to 16 June 2017), and it superseded the interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526. The edition in force at this examination is Rev.2, dated 7 June 2022, which carried an update to the list of additional guidance in paragraph 4.2 approved by MSC 104 and FAL 46.

The Guidelines define maritime cyber risk as a measure of the extent to which a technology asset is threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised (annex 1.1). Note the breadth: corrupted, lost or compromised - loss of availability counts, so a failure with no attacker at all is still a cyber risk.
The Guidelines are expressly recommendatory (annex 2.2.3). Section 7 below explains why that does not make them optional.

blocks.h: 2. The onboard systems exposed to cyber risk

blocks.p: Annex 2.1.1 makes the point the question is quoting: cyber-technologies are essential to systems critical to safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the vulnerabilities created by accessing, interconnecting or networking these systems create cyber risks. The Guidelines say vulnerable systems could include, but are not limited to - so this is a floor, not a closed list:

ul: Bridge systems - ECDIS, radar and ARPA, GNSS receivers, AIS, VDR, the integrated navigation system, autopilot.
Cargo handling and management systems - loading computers and stability software, tanker cargo control, container and reefer monitoring, level and valve control.
Propulsion and machinery management and power control systems - main engine and auxiliary control, the alarm and monitoring system, the power management system, remote OEM diagnostics.
Access control systems - ship security alarm arrangements, CCTV, electronic door and gangway control.
Passenger servicing and management systems - boarding, embarkation and property management systems holding personal and payment data.
Passenger facing public networks - passenger Wi-Fi and entertainment, which are exposed by design.
Administrative and crew welfare systems - the ship business network, planned maintenance and procurement, and crew internet.
Communication systems - satellite communications, the shore link, email and the routers and firewalls between them.

blocks.h: 3. What cyber risk management means, and where it starts

blocks.p: Annex 3.1 defines cyber risk management as the process of identifying, analysing, assessing, and communicating a cyber-related risk and accepting, avoiding, transferring or mitigating it to an acceptable level, considering costs and benefits of actions taken to stakeholders. Two halves: assess the risk, then take one of four decisions about it. The goal (3.2) is to support safe and secure shipping that is operationally resilient to cyber risks - resilience, not immunity.

Annex 3.3 places the starting point: effective cyber risk management should start at the senior management level, which should embed a culture of cyber risk awareness into all levels of the organization and ensure a regime that is holistic and flexible, in continuous operation and constantly evaluated through effective feedback mechanisms. Annex 3.4 gives the accepted method: compare the organization's current and desired postures, and address the gaps through a prioritized cyber risk management plan, so resources go where the risk is. Annex 2.1.9 divides the available controls into management, operational or procedural, and technical.

Annex 3.5 sets out five functional elements, and states that they are not sequential - all should be concurrent and continuous in practice and incorporated appropriately in a risk management framework:

ul: Identify - define personnel roles and responsibilities for cyber risk management, and identify the systems, assets, data and capabilities that, when disrupted, pose risks to ship operations.
Protect - implement risk control processes and measures, and contingency planning, to protect against a cyber-event and ensure continuity of shipping operations.
Detect - develop and implement the activities necessary to detect a cyber-event in a timely manner.
Respond - develop and implement activities and plans to provide resilience and to restore systems necessary for shipping operations or services impaired by a cyber-event.
Recover - identify measures to back up and restore cyber systems necessary for shipping operations impacted by a cyber-event.

blocks.p: Annex 3.6 adds that together they constitute an ongoing process with effective feedback mechanisms, and 3.7 that awareness must be appropriate to each person's role. Writing them out as a five-step sequence to be worked through once is the commonest error on this limb.

blocks.h: 5. Why cyber security matters in the maritime sector

blocks.p: The Guidelines give the reason directly at annex 1.4: risk management has traditionally been focused on the physical domain, and greater reliance on digitization, integration, automation and network-based systems has created an increasing need for cyber risk management in shipping. Four features make the shipping case distinct:

ul: A compromise becomes a safety event. Annex 2.1.5 says so - where critical systems such as bridge navigation or main propulsion are compromised there are implications for safety. Grounding, collision, loss of propulsion and pollution are cyber outcomes, not merely data outcomes.

IT and OT are connected, so an office problem becomes an engine-room problem. Annex 2.1.6 gives the mechanism - inappropriate connection between the two, or a procedural lapse such as the inappropriate use of removable media.
The threat need not be malicious. Annex 2.1.4 puts software maintenance and user permissions alongside hacking and malware.

The ship is hard to defend. Annex 2.1.5 names inadequacies in design, integration and maintenance and lapses in cyberdiscipline - weak passwords, absence of network segregation. Mixed-vendor equipment on long lifecycles, a small rotating crew and a thin satellite link make patching, monitoring and specialist support all harder than ashore.

blocks.p: Annex 2.1.8 draws the management conclusion: technologies and threats change too quickly to be addressed only through technical standards - which is why the answer is a risk-management regime placed inside existing safety and security management practice rather than beside it.

Annex 2.1.2 draws the distinction in one sentence each. Information technology systems may be thought of as focusing on the use of data as information. Operational technology systems may be thought of as focusing on the use of data to control or monitor physical processes. The circular adds that the protection of information and data exchange within these systems should also be considered.

Engine and auxiliary control, alarm and monitoring, power management, steering gear control, ECDIS, radar, GNSS, AIS, ballast water and cargo control

blocks.p: The examinable point is the convergence: the two are no longer separate. A chart update carried aboard on a memory stick, a remote diagnostic session opened to an engine vendor, or a loading computer that reads from the business network all cross the boundary. Network segregation is therefore the single most effective control, and it is the one annex 2.1.5 names when it describes indirect exploitation.

blocks.h: 7. How a recommendatory circular becomes a real obligation

blocks.p: The Guidelines themselves are recommendatory, but the obligation is not. Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017, affirms that an approved safety management system should take cyber risk management into account in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, and encourages Administrations to ensure that cyber risks are appropriately addressed in safety management systems no later than the first annual verification of the company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021.

That date has passed at this examination, so the position is: the guidance on how to manage cyber risk is recommendatory, but whether it is managed at all is an ISM Code matter - verified at DOC and SMC audit and capable of being written up as a non-conformity or a port State control deficiency. For the detail, annex 4.2 points outside the Organization: the industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS Rec 166, ISO/IEC 27001, the NIST Framework and the IAPH port guidelines - and annex 4.3 requires the most current version of whatever is used.

Sixteen marks, four printed limbs, no printed split - so budget four marks each and do not let limb (A) run away with the page. (A) is a list: eight named categories, each worth a few words of shipboard example, and the marks are in the naming. (B) is the heart of the question and is really two things - the definition and posture (annex 3.1 to 3.4) and the five functional elements (3.5). Splitting them, as the route does, stops the answer collapsing into five bullet points. (C) is the only discursive limb; anchor it in the Guidelines' own reasoning rather than in general cyber-security talk. (D) is a two-sentence definition that the Guidelines supply verbatim, and a table earns its marks faster than prose.

blocks.h: The single fact that dates this answer

blocks.p: There are five functional elements at this sitting, not six. The edition in force in March 2024 is Rev.2 of 7 June 2022: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. A sixth element, Govern, was added ahead of Identify by MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3, approved 4 April 2025 - thirteen months after this examination. Material written from 2025 onwards says six, and it is right about today and wrong about this paper.

Current note for a candidate sitting today: the operative edition is now Rev.3 and the answer is six functional elements, beginning with Govern - establish and monitor the organization's cyber risk management strategy, expectations and policy. Everything else in this answer, including the eight system categories, the IT/OT definitions and the MSC.428(98) linkage, carries across unchanged. Check the current revision before you sit.

blocks.h: Why the elements are not a sequence

blocks.p: Annex 3.5 says in terms that the functional elements are not sequential and that all should be concurrent and continuous. That is not a drafting nicety. A ship does not stop identifying while it is protecting; detection runs permanently; and recovery capability - backups, restore procedures, spare configuration - has to be built long before an event, which is impossible if recovery is treated as step five. Say this explicitly and the limb is answered at a management level rather than a checklist level.

blocks.h: IT and OT - the distinction that actually earns the mark

blocks.p: Almost every candidate can say 'IT is computers and OT is machinery'. The Guidelines distinguish them by what the data is for: information versus control or monitoring of a physical process. That formulation is better because it classifies the awkward cases correctly. A loading computer is IT when it produces a stability report and OT when it drives valve and pump control. An alarm and monitoring system is OT even though it controls nothing - it monitors a physical process. The follow-on point is the priority inversion: ashore, confidentiality usually leads; on the plant side, availability and safety lead, which is why you cannot simply apply office IT practice to the engine room.

blocks.h: Where this sits in the wider regulatory picture

blocks.p: Three layers, and keeping them apart is worth a mark. MSC.428(98) is the obligation - cyber risk must be addressed in the SMS. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2 is the recommendatory guidance on how. Industry and class material - the BIMCO-led Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS Rec 166, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST - is the detail, and annex 4.2 names it precisely because the Organization does not intend to write it.

Class requirements were not yet in application at this sitting. IACS unified requirements UR E26 (cyber resilience of ships) and UR E27 (cyber resilience of on-board systems and equipment) had been published, but the original 1 January 2024 application was withdrawn and the revised requirements apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024 - four months after this paper. A candidate who wrote that E26 and E27 were in force in March 2024 would be wrong; a candidate who noted that they were coming, and when, would be showing exactly the currency awareness this subject rewards.

ul: Giving the functional elements as a sequence to be worked through. Annex 3.5 says they are not sequential.
Answering limb (C) with generic cyber-security material - hackers, ransomware, statistics - instead of the shipping-specific reasoning at annex 1.4, 2.1.5 and 2.1.6.
Treating cyber risk as a malicious-attack problem only. Annex 2.1.4 puts software maintenance and user permissions in scope.
Saying the Guidelines are mandatory. They are recommendatory (2.2.3); the obligation comes from MSC.428(98) through the ISM Code.
Listing only three or four vulnerable systems. There are eight named categories and the marks in limb (A) are in naming them.
Forgetting that 2.1.1 says 'could include, but are not limited to' - presenting the eight as a closed list.
Defining OT as 'machinery' rather than by function. It is the use of data to control or monitor a physical process.
Omitting the convergence point in limb (D), which is where the real risk lives.

blocks.p:
"How many elements of cyber risk management are there?" Five, under the edition governing this paper, and they are not sequential. Name the circular and revision you are answering on and the answer cannot be marked wrong.

"Is the ECDIS an IT or an OT system?" OT - it uses data to monitor and support control of a physical process, navigation. It is also connected for chart updating, which is exactly the convergence risk.

"Your ship has no internet. Do the Guidelines apply?" Yes. Annex 2.1.4 covers unintended consequences of benign actions and 2.1.6 covers removable media. An air-gapped ship is infected by memory stick.

"Who owns cyber risk on board?" Annex 3.3 - it starts at senior management level, and awareness must be appropriate to each role (3.7). It is not the ETO's private problem.

"Which IMO instrument makes this mandatory?" None makes the Guidelines mandatory. MSC.428(98) makes cyber risk an ISM Code matter, verified at the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021.

ul: Which circular contains the Guidelines, and which revision applies? MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, Rev.2 of 7 June 2022 at this sitting.

Define maritime cyber risk. A measure of the extent to which a technology asset is threatened by a potential circumstance or event which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised.
Name the five functional elements. Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - concurrent, not sequential.

Name four of the eight vulnerable system categories. Bridge; cargo handling and management; propulsion, machinery management and power control; access control; passenger servicing and management; passenger facing public networks; administrative and crew welfare; communication.
What are the three classes of control option? Management; operational or procedural; technical (annex 2.1.9).
What did MSC.428(98) require, and by when? Cyber risks appropriately addressed in the SMS no later than the first annual verification of the company's DOC after 1 January 2021.
Give one control that reduces IT-to-OT propagation. Network segregation; also control of removable media and of remote vendor access.

blocks.p: For the elements, IPDRR - Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - said as a wheel, not a line. For the eight systems, walk the ship from forward to aft and outward: bridge, cargo, machinery, access, passenger service, passenger network, admin and welfare, communications - navigate, carry, propel, control entry, serve passengers, entertain them, run the business, talk to shore. For limb (D), one word each: IT is information, OT is control.
