blocks.h: 1. The resolution, and what made electronic record books lawful

blocks.p: Resolution MEPC.312(74), adopted 17 May 2019, contains the Guidelines for the use of electronic record books under MARPOL. The Guidelines did not by themselves permit anything: at the same session the Committee adopted MEPC.314(74), MEPC.316(74) and MEPC.317(74), which amended MARPOL Annexes I, II, V and VI and the NOx Technical Code 2008 to enable the use of electronic record books. The amendments entered into force 1 October 2020.

The division of labour matters. MARPOL creates the permission; the resolution tells the Administration how to decide whether a particular system may be approved. An electronic record book is expressly an alternative method to a hard copy record book (annex 2.2), not a relaxation of what must be recorded.

blocks.h: 2. The record books that may be kept electronically

blocks.p: Annex 2.1 lists seven record books and recording requirements, and the Guidelines apply only to these:

ul: Oil Record Book, Parts I and II - MARPOL Annex I, regulations 17.1 and 36.1;
Cargo Record Book - MARPOL Annex II, regulation 15.1;
Garbage Record Book, Parts I and II - MARPOL Annex V, regulation 10.3;
Ozone-depleting Substances Record Book - MARPOL Annex VI, regulation 12.6;
recording of the tier and on/off status of marine diesel engines - MARPOL Annex VI, regulation 13.5.3;
Record of Fuel Oil Changeover - MARPOL Annex VI, regulation 14.6; and
Record Book of Engine Parameters - NOx Technical Code, paragraph 6.2.2.7.

blocks.p: Two boundaries are worth stating because they are commonly crossed. The Guidelines do not cover electronic access to, or electronic versions of, certificates and other documents that do not log continuous operations (annex 2.3); and they do not address ship-to-office transmission of the data, because that is not a MARPOL record book requirement at all (annex 2.4). The Ballast Water Record Book is not in the list - it is not a MARPOL instrument.

blocks.h: 3. How the electronic log book meets the MARPOL requirements

blocks.p: Annex 4.1 is the answer to limb (b), and its principle is that the output must satisfy the requirements of all relevant regulations under MARPOL (4.1.1). Four mechanisms deliver that:

ul: Complete entries only. The system should allow only a complete entry to be saved for the master's verification. The resolution's own example: for an Annex V discharge at sea, the entry cannot be saved without the latitude and longitude (4.1.2).

Protected automatic inputs. Where data can be captured automatically it should be, to ensure accuracy; those inputs must be protected against manipulation or falsification; manual entry is allowed on equipment failure but the change of data source must be recorded; and the system must automatically record any attempt to manipulate or falsify data (4.1.2).

The MARPOL form is preserved. Entry fields and data formats should be consistent with other IMO electronic reporting, and the record book should be presented in the form specified in the relevant MARPOL Annex (4.1.3).

Retention and hard copy. The system must retain records for the minimum period specified in each Annex, and must be able to produce a hard copy of verified records for the master to certify as a true copy on request (4.1.4).

blocks.p: Annex 4.2 adds an obligation that a paper book never had: because MARPOL and its Annexes continue to evolve, approved systems must be reviewed and updated so that relevant amendments are incorporated, and the update must be completed before the amendment enters into force. Crucially, an update must not cause loss of existing records nor make them unreadable, and the system must continue to present all records in the MARPOL form. A software product therefore carries a continuing compliance burden that a printed book does not.

Annex 4.4 handles the physical side: the record book must form part of the Information Technology Business Continuity Plan, with backup, data recovery and alternate power supplies; automatic backup to offline storage updated every time an entry changes; the offline record protected by cryptography, held read-only, transferable, durable and printable; that offline record digitally signed by the master with title, full name, date and time of signing, PDF recommended; and the equipment installed in compliance with IEC 60092 and IEC 60533.

blocks.h: 5. Security - access control and audit logging

blocks.p: Annex 4.3 is headed Security and accountability of the electronic record book and answers limb (c) directly. Security rests on two mechanisms:

ul: Role Based Access Control is critical, and at a minimum every user must have a unique personal login identifier and password. The resolution states the purpose plainly: this is what makes the user making an entry accountable for any false entries or omissions (4.3.1).

Audit Logging replaces the officer's signature that MARPOL requires. The log must record a user code or identifying symbol against each entry, uniquely identifying the user and whether that user accessed or amended an entry (4.3.2). Electronic signatures must meet authentication standards adopted by the Administration (4.3.3).

blocks.p: Entries must be protected against unauthorized deletion, destruction or amendment. Once saved, the information must be secured against unauthorized or untraceable change; any change must be automatically recorded and made visible in the system and in any printed output; and - the load-bearing sentence - the system must retain both the original entry and every amendment (4.3.4). An amendment should carry a reason and the user identifier of the officer making it (4.3.5).

blocks.h: 6. Accountability - verification and the status of an entry

blocks.p: MARPOL requires verification, not merely entry - Annex I regulation 17 requires each page of the Oil Record Book to be signed by the master. The Guidelines reproduce that in software:

ul: The master's verification requires an additional authentication factor - further credentials supplied by the master at the time of verification (4.3.6).
The system logs when entries were made, amended or verified, which exposes the practice of entering days or weeks of operations at once (4.3.7).
Each entry carries a status field - 'pending' or 'awaiting verification', becoming 'verified' once the master signs (4.3.8).
If a verified entry is later amended, the system automatically returns it to pending or re-verification and notifies the master (4.3.9).
The system reminds the master that verification is due, ideally before arrival in port, and unverified entries must carry a comment giving the reason (4.3.10).
Receipts and endorsements - a waste reception facility receipt, a Cargo Record Book endorsement - may be identified or attached to the relevant entry (4.3.11).

blocks.p: A system meeting the criteria is given written confirmation by the Administration, which must be carried on board for surveys and inspections - in practice the Declaration of MARPOL Electronic Record Book at the appendix, naming the ship, IMO number, flag, gross tonnage, the Annexes covered, and the manufacturer, supplier, installer, software name and version (annex 5.1). The Administration may delegate the assessment and the issue of the declaration to a recognized organization, at its discretion (5.2).

At inspection, the system must meet company audit requirements including integration with the ISM Code safety management system, all flag State and survey requirements, the MARPOL control provisions and the Organization's port State control procedures, and must support detection of violations under MARPOL article 6 (6.1.1). Using an electronic book in no way relieves the owner of the duty to maintain and produce records; if the ship can produce neither the system nor the declaration, the officer should ask for an alternative verified copy or a hard copy book (6.1.2). For prosecution, any entry or the whole book must be printable and each page physically signed by the master as a 'true copy', carrying the entering officer's title and full name, any changes made, the date and time of printing, the system name and version, and page numbering (6.3).

Sixteen marks, three limbs, no printed split - so roughly five marks each, and limb (a) is the one that can be answered perfectly in six lines. It is a closed list of seven, and the marks are in naming them with their Annex and regulation. Do not spend a page on it. Limb (b) is the conceptual limb: the system meets MARPOL because it forces completeness, preserves the MARPOL form, retains for the statutory period and can produce a certified hard copy. Limb (c) is the richest and the resolution has a section with exactly that title - annex 4.3, Security and accountability - so a candidate who has read it can out-answer everyone else.

blocks.h: The list is seven, and it is not the list most people give

blocks.p: This is where the question is won or lost. Automated summaries of this very resolution get the list wrong - one consulted during research offered the Ballast Water Record Book (not a MARPOL instrument at all), 'engine maintenance and fuel consumption logs' (not a MARPOL record), and omitted the Cargo Record Book, the ODS Record Book and the NOx Technical Code engine parameter book entirely. The correct seven come from annex 2.1 and nowhere else. Notice the shape of the list: three classic record books (Oil, Cargo, Garbage), three Annex VI items (ODS, engine tier and on/off status, fuel oil changeover) and one from the NOx Technical Code.

blocks.h: Why the amendment obligation is the interesting part of limb (b)

blocks.p: A paper record book is compliant on the day it is printed and stays compliant because it cannot change. Software has the opposite property. Annex 4.2 therefore imposes something no paper book carries: the approved system must be updated before the relevant MARPOL amendment enters into force, without losing or corrupting the existing records. That converts a one-off approval into a continuing obligation shared between the supplier, the company and the Administration, and it is a genuinely management-level observation - exactly the register this paper is set in.

blocks.h: Security and accountability are two different things

blocks.p: Candidates blur them. Security is about keeping the record trustworthy - role based access control, unique credentials, cryptography on the offline copy, protection against unauthorized deletion or amendment. Accountability is about being able to say who did what and when - the audit log against each entry, the master's separate authentication factor, the pending/verified status, and above all the rule that both the original entry and every amendment are retained and visible. That last rule is what makes the electronic book stronger evidence than paper, where a neat line through an entry destroys the original.

Oil Record Book falsification is the most heavily prosecuted MARPOL offence there is, and annex 6.3 is written for the courtroom: the printed page must be signed by the master as a true copy and must show any changes that were made, the software name and version, and the print date and time. A Chief Engineer should read that as follows - with an approved electronic book, an amendment is not a correction, it is a permanent record of a correction. That is a protection for an honest engineer and an exposure for a careless one.

ul: Listing the Ballast Water Record Book. It is a BWM Convention document, not MARPOL, and is not in annex 2.1.

Giving only the Oil and Garbage Record Books. There are seven items, including the Cargo Record Book, the ODS Record Book, engine tier and on/off status, fuel oil changeover, and the NOx Technical Code engine parameter book.

Saying MEPC.312(74) permits electronic record books. It does not - the MARPOL amendments adopted by MEPC.314(74), MEPC.316(74) and MEPC.317(74) do, in force 1 October 2020. The resolution is the approval guidance.
Treating the electronic book as a relaxation. Annex 2.2 calls it an alternative method; every MARPOL recording requirement still applies.
Forgetting the Declaration that must be carried on board, and that a ship which can produce neither system nor declaration will be asked for a hard copy.
Saying an incorrect entry is deleted or corrected. Both the original and the amendment are retained and visible.
Omitting the master's separate authentication factor - it is what replaces the signature MARPOL requires.
Claiming the Guidelines cover transmission of data to the office. Annex 2.4 says they do not.

blocks.p:
"Name all the record books that can be electronic." Seven, and the word all in the question means the examiner is counting.

"Can the Chief Engineer correct a wrong entry?" Yes, and the correction is permanent and visible: the amendment is recorded with reason and user identifier, the original is retained, and a verified entry returns to pending for the master to re-verify.

"The PSCO asks for the Oil Record Book and the tablet will not start." Annex 6.1.2 - the officer should ask for an alternative verified copy or a hard copy, and the duty to produce records is unaffected. This is why annex 4.4.1 requires backup, recovery and alternate power supplies.

"Who approves the system?" The Administration, which may delegate the assessment and the declaration to a recognized organization.

"What must appear on a printed page for a prosecution?" The entering officer's title and full name, any changes made, date and time of printing, software name and version, and page numbering - plus the master's physical signature certifying it a true copy.

ul: Which resolution contains the Guidelines and when was it adopted? MEPC.312(74), 17 May 2019.
What made electronic record books lawful, and when? The MARPOL amendments adopted by MEPC.314(74), MEPC.316(74) and MEPC.317(74) - in force 1 October 2020.
Which regulation covers the Oil Record Book Parts I and II? MARPOL Annex I, regulations 17.1 and 36.1.
What two mechanisms give security? Role Based Access Control with unique credentials, and Audit Logging against every entry.
How does the master verify an entry? With an additional authentication factor - further credentials supplied at the time of verification.
What happens if a verified entry is amended? It automatically returns to pending or re-verification and the master is notified.
What document proves the system is approved? The Declaration of MARPOL Electronic Record Book, carried on board.
To which standards must the installation comply? IEC 60092 and IEC 60533.

questions.understand_first: The real question is how you make a computer satisfy a rule that was written assuming paper and a pen. MARPOL wanted a bound book, entries in a fixed form, an officer's signature against each one and the master's signature on each page, kept for years and producible to an inspector. Every requirement in these Guidelines is one of those paper properties rebuilt in software - and the interesting result is that two of them come out stronger than paper, because the system records who did it and keeps what the entry used to say.
questions.memory_cue: Follow one entry through its life and you have the whole answer. It is made in one of seven books (2), it cannot be saved incomplete and it looks like the MARPOL form (3), it is signed for by a named user under role based access (5), the master verifies it with his own credentials and it turns from pending to verified (6), any later change is kept alongside the original (5), it survives update and power failure (4), and it can be printed and certified for an inspector (7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name all the record books and recording requirements that may be kept electronically.
retrieval_cards.answer: Seven: Oil Record Book Parts I and II (Annex I regs 17.1, 36.1); Cargo Record Book (Annex II reg 15.1); Garbage Record Book Parts I and II (Annex V reg 10.3); Ozone-depleting Substances Record Book (Annex VI reg 12.6); recording of tier and on/off status of marine diesel engines (Annex VI reg 13.5.3); Record of Fuel Oil Changeover (Annex VI reg 14.6); Record Book of Engine Parameters (NOx Technical Code para 6.2.2.7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Ballast Water Record Book covered by MEPC.312(74)?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is a BWM Convention document, not a MARPOL record book, and does not appear in annex 2.1.
retrieval_cards.why: A published summary of this very resolution listed it - opening the source is what caught it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did MEPC.312(74) make electronic record books lawful?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The MARPOL amendments adopted by MEPC.314(74), MEPC.316(74) and MEPC.317(74) enabled them, in force 1 October 2020. MEPC.312(74) is guidance to Administrations on approving a system.
retrieval_cards.why: Permission and approval guidance are different instruments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What two mechanisms does annex 4.3 rely on for security?
retrieval_cards.answer: Role Based Access Control - at minimum a unique personal login identifier and password for every user - and Audit Logging, recording a user code or identifying symbol against each entry and whether the user accessed or amended it.
retrieval_cards.why: RBAC is what makes the user accountable for false entries or omissions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can an incorrect entry simply be corrected in an electronic record book?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Both the original entry and every amendment must be retained and made visible, in the system and in any printed output, with the reason and the user identifier recorded. A verified entry that is amended returns automatically to pending or re-verification.
retrieval_cards.why: This is why an electronic book is stronger evidence than paper, where a struck-through entry destroys the original.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the master verify entries, and what does the system show?
retrieval_cards.answer: With an additional authentication factor - further credentials supplied at the time of verification. Each entry carries a status field: pending or awaiting verification, then verified. The system reminds the master, ideally before arrival in port.
retrieval_cards.why: MARPOL requires the master's signature; this is its software equivalent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What proves that an electronic record book is approved, and who issues it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Written confirmation from the Administration, carried on board - in practice the Declaration of MARPOL Electronic Record Book. The Administration may delegate the assessment and issue to a recognized organization at its discretion.
retrieval_cards.why: Annex 5. A ship that can produce neither system nor declaration will be asked for a hard copy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must appear on a printed page produced for a prosecution?
retrieval_cards.answer: The title and full name of the person who entered the record, any changes made to the entries, the date and time of printing, the name and version of the electronic record book, and page numbering with the number of pages - and each page physically signed by the master certifying it a true copy.
retrieval_cards.why: Annex 6.3, written for the courtroom.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must happen to an approved system when MARPOL is amended?
retrieval_cards.answer: It must be reviewed and updated so the amendment is incorporated, completed before the amendment enters into force, without causing loss of existing records or making them unreadable.
retrieval_cards.why: Annex 4.2 - a continuing compliance obligation a paper book never carried.

blocks.h: 1. The Code, and what made it mandatory

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) is the annex to resolution A.1070(28), adopted by the Assembly on 4 December 2013. It revoked resolution A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011 (operative paragraph 3), which had been the basis of the voluntary audit scheme.

The Code is recommendatory in its own drafting - it says what a State "should" do - but its use was made mandatory by amendments to the treaty instruments themselves: A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) amended Load Lines 1966, Tonnage 1969 and COLREG 1972; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) amended SOLAS 1974, STCW 1978, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; and MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) amended MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol. That chain is what turns the Code into the standard against which a Member State is audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme.

The Code has four parts: Part 1 Common Areas, Part 2 Flag States, Part 3 Coastal States and Part 4 Port States. Each of Parts 2, 3 and 4 ends with an Evaluation and review section, which is where limb (b) lives.

Paragraph 1 states the objective in one sentence: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization. The second half matters as much as the first - the Code is an assistance instrument, written because the Organization accepted that some States face real difficulty in complying fully.

Paragraph 2 qualifies it. Different States will view the Code according to their own circumstances and should be bound only for the implementation of those instruments to which they are Contracting Governments or Parties; by virtue of geography and circumstance some States have a greater role as a flag State, others as a coastal or port State. The Code is therefore not a uniform checklist applied identically everywhere.

Two general provisions frame everything that follows. Paragraph 4 makes States responsible for promulgating laws and regulations and taking all other steps necessary to give those instruments full and complete effect. Paragraph 5 requires that, in acting against pollution, States must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, nor transform one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: 3. The strategy recommended to the flag State

blocks.p: Paragraph 3 is the answer to the second half of limb (a). To meet the objective, a State is recommended to:

ul: develop an overall strategy to ensure that its international obligations and responsibilities as a flag, port and coastal State are met (3.1);
establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy ensures effective implementation and enforcement of relevant international mandatory instruments (3.2); and
continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve overall organizational performance and capability as a flag, port and coastal State (3.3).

blocks.p: Read together those three are a develop - monitor - review cycle, not a document to be written once. Paragraph 9 completes it: the State should communicate its strategy, including information on its national legislation, to all concerned.

Paragraph 7 tells the State what its legislation and administrative procedures must actually address - nine areas: jurisdiction; organization and authority; legislation, rules and regulations; promulgation of the applicable mandatory instruments; enforcement arrangements; control, survey, inspection, audit, verification, approval and certification functions; the selection, recognition, authorization, empowerment and monitoring of recognized organizations and nominated surveyors; investigations required to be reported to the Organization; and reporting to the Organization and other Administrations. Paragraph 8 adds the three initial actions a Government must be capable of when a new or amended instrument enters into force: the ability to promulgate laws giving effective jurisdiction and control, a legal basis for enforcement including investigative and penal processes, and sufficient personnel with maritime expertise.

blocks.h: 4. Which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: This limb has two correct answers and they are not the same, which is where marks are usually lost.
First, the Code's own scope. Paragraph 6 says the Code addresses those aspects necessary to give full and complete effect to the applicable international instruments pertaining to six subject areas:

ul: safety of life at sea;
prevention of pollution from ships;
standards of training, certification and watchkeeping for seafarers;
load lines;
tonnage measurement of ships; and
regulations for preventing collisions at sea.

blocks.p: Note what is absent: maritime security is not one of the six. The preamble to the resolution speaks of safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the operative scope at paragraph 6 does not extend to the ISPS Code or SOLAS chapter XI-2.

Second, the treaty instruments under which use of the Code is mandatory, and which therefore define the audit scope. These are the instruments listed in resolution A.1187(33) (6 December 2023), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code: SOLAS 1974 with its 1978 and 1988 Protocols; MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; Tonnage 1969; and COLREG 1972. A.1187(33) revoked the 2021 list, A.1157(32), so it is the current list at this sitting; its annexes divide the obligations into those of Contracting Governments generally and those specific to flag, coastal and port States.

blocks.h: 5. Key performance indicators for flag State evaluation

blocks.p: Paragraph 42 requires a flag State to evaluate its performance on a periodic basis with respect to the administrative processes, procedures and resources needed to meet its obligations. Paragraph 43 then lists the measures, inter alia:

ul: port State control detention rates;
flag State inspection results;
casualty statistics;
communication and information processes;
annual loss statistics, excluding constructive total losses (CTLs); and
such other performance indicators as may be appropriate.

blocks.p: The stated purpose is diagnostic, and quoting it earns the mark: the indicators exist in order to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet its flag State obligations.

Paragraph 44 then recommends ten areas for regular review: fleet loss and accident ratios, to identify trends over selected time periods; the number of verified cases of detained ships in relation to the size of the fleet; verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by holders of certificates or endorsements issued under its authority; responses to port State deficiency reports or interventions; investigations into very serious and serious casualties and the lessons learned; technical and other resources committed; results of inspections, surveys and controls of ships in the fleet; investigation of occupational accidents; the number of incidents and violations under the applicable international pollution prevention regulations; and the number of suspensions or withdrawals of certificates, endorsements or approvals.
Part 2 is the longest part of the Code, paragraphs 15 to 44. Its structure is implementation - delegation - enforcement - surveyors - investigations - review.

ul: Implementation (15-17). Issue national legislation and guidance implementing the safety and pollution conventions, and assign responsibility for keeping it updated. Paragraph 16 requires a safety and environmental protection programme with five minimum elements, of which the load-bearing one is 16.2: compliance verified by an audit and inspection programme independent of any body issuing the certificates. Paragraph 17 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned, on the Principles of Safe Manning.

Delegation of authority (18-21). A flag State authorising a recognized organization must determine that it has adequate technical, managerial and research capability; base the authorisation on a formal written agreement; issue specific instructions for a ship found unfit to proceed to sea; supply its national law and interpretations; and require the organization to keep records. Paragraph 20 requires an oversight programme with supplementary surveys and competent supervising staff.

Enforcement (22-27). Prohibit a ship from sailing until it complies; inspect periodically to verify that the actual condition of ship and crew matches the certificates; verify seafarer familiarity and the complement's ability to coordinate in an emergency; provide penalties of adequate severity for ships and for certificate holders; and institute proceedings after investigation irrespective of where the violation occurred. Paragraphs 26 and 27 permit certification only after determining that all applicable requirements are met.

Surveyors and investigations (28-41). Surveyors must be qualified against a defined standard, worked under a documented qualification system, and issued an identification document. Marine safety investigations must be by impartial and objective investigators; casualties are investigated taking account of the Casualty Investigation Code and the report is forwarded to the Organization with the flag State's observations.

blocks.h: 7. Coastal State and port State responsibilities

blocks.p: Parts 3 and 4 open with the same principle, at paragraphs 45 and 52: coastal and port States have rights as well as obligations, and when they exercise those rights they incur additional obligations. Both must implement policy through national legislation and guidance (46, 54) and ensure their legislation and procedures deliver consistent implementation and verification (47, 55).

Coastal State (Part 3). Paragraph 48 lists the rights, obligations and responsibilities, inter alia: radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation - eight service areas, and note that they are services to shipping, not controls over ships. Paragraph 50 requires a control and monitoring programme to allocate statistical data for trend analysis, to establish mechanisms for timely response to pollution incidents in its waters, and to cooperate with flag and port States in casualty investigations.

Port State (Part 4). Paragraph 53 records that the port State role derives from a combination of treaties, conventions, national laws and in some cases bilateral and multilateral agreements. Paragraph 56 gives three obligations: provision of appropriate reception facilities or capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers. Paragraph 59 carries the no more favourable treatment principle - the port State must impose the conditions of those instruments on non-parties as well as parties. Paragraphs 60 and 61 require a PSC programme consistent with the relevant Assembly resolution, carried out only by authorized and qualified port State control officers; paragraph 62 requires those officers to be free from commercial, financial and other pressures, to hold no commercial interest in the port, the ships inspected, repair facilities or support services, and not to be employed by or work on behalf of recognized organizations or classification societies.

Both parts close as Part 2 does: paragraphs 51 and 63 require the coastal State and the port State to periodically evaluate their own performance in exercising their rights and meeting their obligations. That symmetry - implement, enforce, evaluate - is the single most useful thing to carry into the exam hall, because it lets you structure all three States from one remembered shape.

The printed marks are 6 + 4 + 6 and the question hides four tasks inside limb (a): objective, strategy, instruments, and the implied "what is this Code". Splitting (a) across route steps 2, 3 and 4 stops the six marks being spent on a single paragraph about the objective. Limb (b) is only four marks but has a precise source - paragraphs 43 and 44 - so a candidate who names the indicators verbatim banks those marks quickly and buys time for limb (c).

Limb (c) covers three States in six marks. Two marks each. The Code makes that easy because Parts 2, 3 and 4 share a skeleton: implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. Answer all three on that skeleton and the examiner sees structure rather than a list.

blocks.h: The mandatory-application chain, and why it matters

blocks.p: Candidates often assert that "the III Code is mandatory" without being able to say why a recommendatory-sounding text binds anybody. The answer is that the Code itself was never redrafted into obligation language; instead the conventions were amended to require its use. That is why the Code still reads "should" throughout. Being able to say this in one sentence distinguishes a candidate who has read the instrument from one who has read about it.

The audit scheme is the practical consequence. The Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligation-by-obligation list that auditors and Administrations work from. A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, replacing the 2021 list, A.1157(32) - three months before this sitting. Material citing the 2021 list is superseded.

The printed words are "Which all IMO instruments covered in the code". Two things are being asked at once and the safe answer gives both. The Code's scope at paragraph 6 is expressed as six subject areas, not as a list of conventions. The instruments under which the Code is mandatory are the SOLAS / MARPOL / STCW / Load Lines / Tonnage / COLREG family with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33).

A count is risky. The audit scope is usually summarised as nine mandatory instruments - SOLAS 1974, SOLAS PROT 1988, MARPOL, MARPOL PROT 1997, STCW 1978, LL 1966, LL PROT 1988, TONNAGE 1969 and COLREG 1972 - but A.1187(33) annex 1 also carries a SOLAS PROT 1978 column, and neither the Code nor A.1187(33) states a number anywhere. List them; do not lead with a count. If a count is wanted, say "the SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG instruments together with their Protocols, commonly summarised as nine".

The absence of maritime security from paragraph 6 is a genuine examinable point, not a drafting slip: the preamble uses the phrase "safety, security and protection of the marine environment" while the operative scope does not extend to security instruments.

ul: Writing a general essay on flag State duties under UNCLOS article 94. That is a different question. The examiner has named a specific Code and wants its paragraphs.
Answering limb (a)'s "which instruments" with the six subject areas only, or with the convention list only. Give both and say why they differ.
Confusing the III Code with the ISM Code. The III Code binds States; the ISM Code binds companies and ships.
Treating the performance indicators as something the flag State reports to IMO. They are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation under paragraph 42.
Giving the coastal State a control-and-inspection role. Paragraph 48 is a list of services - SAR, hydrography, VTS, aids to navigation.
Spending half the answer on limb (c) because it is familiar. It is worth six marks, the same as limb (a).
Six subject areas versus the instrument list. The single most likely place to lose marks on this question.
"Should" throughout the Code. If asked whether the Code is mandatory, the answer is that its use is mandatory under the amended conventions, while the text remains recommendatory in form.
Excluding constructive total losses. Paragraph 43 says annual loss statistics excluding CTLs. Reproducing that qualifier shows the source has been read.

Independence. Two independence requirements appear, in different Parts and for different reasons - the flag State's audit programme must be independent of the certifying body (16.2), and PSCOs must be free of commercial interest and not work for recognized organizations (62). Do not merge them.
A.1054(27) was revoked. An answer that cites the 2011 Code as current is citing a revoked instrument.
"Is the III Code mandatory, and how?" - use the amendment chain.
"What is IMSAS and what does it audit against?" - the Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligations list.

"Your flag State has a rising detention rate. What does the Code expect it to do?" - paragraphs 43 and 44: treat it as a performance indicator, review detentions against fleet size, review responses to PSC deficiency reports, and test whether staffing and resources are adequate.

"What must a flag State do before authorising a class society?" - paragraph 18: capability, a formal written agreement, specific instructions for unfit ships, national law and interpretations, records.
"Name three port State obligations under the Code." - reception facilities, port State control, register of fuel oil suppliers.

"Which State investigates a casualty, and who gets the report?" - paragraphs 38 and 41: the flag State provides qualified investigators irrespective of casualty location; the report goes to the Organization with the flag State's observations.

blocks.p: Two shapes carry the whole question. The Code's shape is common areas, then flag, then coastal, then port. The shape inside each State part is implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. Everything in limb (c) hangs on the second shape, and limb (b) is simply the "evaluation and review" box of the flag State part opened up.

For the coastal State's eight services, group them as talk, warn, rescue, chart (radiocommunication, meteorological warnings, SAR, hydrographic) and route, report, watch, mark (ships' routeing, ship reporting, VTS, aids to navigation).

blocks.h: Flag State surveyors and investigations - the detail behind route step 6

blocks.p: Limb (c) is six marks for three States, so the Model Answer gives the flag State the headline of paragraphs 28 to 41 rather than the whole regime. The detail below is worth holding for the oral, and for any future question that asks about surveyor competence directly.

ul: Qualification (para 29). Either appropriate qualifications from a marine or nautical institution with relevant seagoing experience as a certificated officer holding or having held a valid management level certificate of competency, with maintained technical knowledge; or a degree or equivalent from a tertiary institution in a relevant field of engineering or science recognised by the flag State; or accreditation as a surveyor through a formalised training programme reaching the same standard.

Experience (paras 30-31). Personnel qualified under 29.1 should have served not less than three years at sea as a deck or engine officer; those qualified under 29.2 should have worked in a relevant capacity for at least three years.

Knowledge (para 36). The qualification should encompass knowledge of the applicable international and national rules; of survey, certification, control, investigative and oversight procedures; understanding of the goals of the instruments and of the processes both on board and ashore; professional competency; full safety awareness; and training or experience in the tasks performed.
Identification (para 37). The flag State issues an identification document for the surveyor to carry when performing his or her tasks.

Investigator expertise (para 39). Ready access is required to expertise in navigation and the Collision Regulations, flag State certificate-of-competency regulations, causes of marine pollution, interviewing techniques, evidence gathering, and evaluation of the effects of the human element.

Reporting threshold (para 40). Any accident involving personal injury necessitating absence from duty of three days or more, and any deaths resulting from occupational accidents and casualties, should be investigated and the results made public.

blocks.p: The answer deliberately does not lead with a number of instruments. A.1070(28) states six subject areas and states no instrument count; A.1187(33) lists obligations by instrument without totalling them. The figure of nine is a widely used summary of the mandatory instruments and is offered as such, not as a quotation from either resolution. A candidate who writes "nine" will not be marked wrong, but a candidate who lists the instruments cannot be.

The Framework and Procedures for the Member State Audit Scheme was not re-read for this answer, so no claim is made here about audit periodicity or about the scheme's own procedural rules. The answer restricts itself to what the Code and the obligations list say.

The Code is short - sixty-three paragraphs in four parts - and it is organised exactly the way the question is: common material first, then flag, coastal and port States in that order, each ending with an evaluation and review section. retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Code and what made it mandatory. 2 (a) The objective. 3 (a) The strategy. 4 (a) Which instruments. 5 (b) The performance indicators. 6 (c) Flag State. 7 (c) Coastal and port State.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution contains the III Code, when was it adopted, and what did it revoke?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013. Operative paragraph 3 revoked A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the revoked 2011 Code as current is a common and visible error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the objective of the III Code in the Code's own words.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 1: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The second half - assistance - is routinely dropped, and it is half the sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What three things does paragraph 3 recommend a State do to meet the objective?
retrieval_cards.answer: Develop an overall strategy covering its flag, port and coastal responsibilities; establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy delivers effective implementation and enforcement; and continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve organizational performance and capability.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the "strategy recommended to flag state" half of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: The question asks which IMO instruments the Code covers. Why are there two answers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 6 defines the Code's scope as six SUBJECT AREAS - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution from ships, STCW, load lines, tonnage measurement, COLREG. Separately, the Code is made mandatory by amendments to the treaty INSTRUMENTS - SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and its Code, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Give both.
retrieval_cards.why: The highest-value distinction on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which subject area is conspicuously absent from paragraph 6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maritime security. The preamble speaks of safety, security and environmental protection, but the six subject areas in the operative scope do not include security, so the ISPS Code and SOLAS chapter XI-2 sit outside the Code's stated scope.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who lists seven areas including security has not read paragraph 6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the flag State performance indicators at paragraph 43.
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control detention rates; flag State inspection results; casualty statistics; communication and information processes; annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses; and other appropriate indicators. Their purpose is to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) is four marks and this paragraph is the whole of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two independence requirements appear in the Code. What are they and where?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 16.2 - the flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of any body issuing the certificates, including a delegated entity. Paragraph 62 - port State control officers must be free of commercial, financial and other pressure, hold no commercial interest in the port or ships inspected, and not be employed by or work for recognized organizations or classification societies.
retrieval_cards.why: They serve different purposes in different Parts and are often merged into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the eight coastal State areas at paragraph 48.
retrieval_cards.answer: Radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation.
retrieval_cards.why: They are services to shipping, not controls over ships - which is the point of Part 3.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three port State obligations at paragraph 56.
retrieval_cards.answer: Provision of appropriate reception facilities, or the capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers.
retrieval_cards.why: The register of fuel oil suppliers is the one candidates forget.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Code says "should" throughout. How is it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code was not redrafted into obligation language. Its USE was made mandatory by amendments to the conventions - A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) for Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) for SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) for MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol.

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and how it is built

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 was adopted at the 94th (Maritime) Session of the International Labour Conference. It consolidated some sixty-eight earlier ILO maritime instruments into one, and is universally described as the fourth pillar of the international regulatory regime, standing beside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW. It is often called the seafarers' bill of rights.

Its architecture is unusual and is worth a sentence in any answer. It has three parts: the Articles, which set out the general obligations; the Regulations; and the Code. Article VI then divides the Code in two - Part A contains Standards and is mandatory, while Part B contains Guidelines which are not mandatory but to which Members must give due consideration. Article VI.3 adds the flexibility mechanism of substantial equivalence: a Member may implement a Part A Standard differently provided the provision is substantially equivalent in achieving the general object and purpose.

The Regulations and Code are arranged in five Titles: Title 1 minimum requirements to work on a ship; Title 2 conditions of employment; Title 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; Title 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; and Title 5 compliance and enforcement. Article IV states the underlying rights: a safe and secure workplace, fair terms of employment, decent working and living conditions, and health protection, medical care, welfare measures and other forms of social protection.

The text in force at this sitting is the Convention as amended by the 2014, 2016 and 2018 amendments, approved at the 103rd, 105th and 107th Sessions of the Conference respectively. Those three amendment sets are the ones an answer may rely on.

blocks.h: 2. Minimum requirements and the employment agreement

blocks.p: Title 1 controls who may go to sea.

ul: Minimum age (Reg 1.1). Standard A1.1.1 - the employment, engagement or work on board of any person under the age of 16 is prohibited. A1.1.2 - night work by seafarers under 18 is prohibited, "night" covering a period of at least nine hours starting no later than midnight and ending no earlier than 5 a.m. Hazardous work by those under 18 is likewise prohibited.

Medical fitness (Reg 1.2). A valid medical certificate is required before beginning work. Standard A1.2.7 - it is valid for a maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18, and a certification of colour vision for a maximum of six years. An STCW medical certificate is accepted.

Training and recruitment (Regs 1.3 and 1.4). Seafarers must be trained and qualified for their duties, and recruitment and placement services must be regulated - notably, no fees are to be borne by the seafarer.

blocks.p: The seafarers' employment agreement (Reg 2.1) is the document the question names first. Standard A2.1.1 requires an agreement signed by both the seafarer and the shipowner or a representative, providing decent working and living conditions; the seafarer must be given an opportunity to examine it and to seek advice before signing, so that the agreement is freely entered into. Both parties hold a signed original, a copy is carried on board and available to the seafarer and to inspectors, and the seafarer receives a record of employment which contains no statement as to the quality of the work or the wages.

blocks.h: 3. Hours, wages, leave, repatriation and manning

blocks.p: Hours of work and rest (Reg 2.3) is the provision most tested in practice. Standard A2.3.3 sets the baseline at an eight-hour day with one day of rest per week and rest on public holidays. A2.3.5 then requires each Member to fix either a maximum number of hours of work or a minimum number of hours of rest:

ul: maximum hours of work - not exceeding 14 hours in any 24-hour period and 72 hours in any seven-day period; or
minimum hours of rest - not less than ten hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any seven-day period.

blocks.p: Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which must be at least six hours, with no more than fourteen hours between consecutive rest periods. A2.3.4 requires national standards to take account of the danger posed by fatigue, especially for those with navigational duties. A table of shipboard working arrangements is posted and records of daily hours are kept.

Wages (Reg 2.2) are paid at intervals no greater than monthly, with a monthly account and a means of transmitting allotments home. Leave (Reg 2.4) gives paid annual leave, and Reg 2.7 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned. Repatriation (Reg 2.5) is the seafarer's ultimate protection: Standard A2.5.1 gives entitlement when the agreement expires while abroad, when it is terminated by the shipowner or by the seafarer for justified reasons, and when the seafarer can no longer carry out the duties. A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period on board after which repatriation falls due to be less than twelve months. Since the 2014 amendments, in force at this sitting, the shipowner must also maintain financial security for abandonment, evidenced by a certificate carried on board; and since the 2018 amendments a seafarer's wages continue during captivity following piracy or armed robbery.

blocks.h: 4. Accommodation, catering, health, welfare and social security

ul: Accommodation and recreational facilities (Reg 3.1). Accommodation must be safe and decent, with detailed requirements for size, headroom, heating, ventilation, lighting, sanitary facilities and hospital accommodation. Note the application rule: the construction standards apply only to ships built on or after the Convention entered into force for that Member. Accommodation is inspected on board at frequent, recorded intervals.

Food and catering (Reg 3.2). Food and drinking water of appropriate quality, nutritional value and quantity, supplied free of charge during the period of engagement; ships' cooks must be trained and qualified, and no seafarer under 18 may serve as ship's cook.

Medical care (Reg 4.1). Health protection and medical care comparable to that available ashore, provided free of charge, including the right to visit a qualified doctor or dentist without delay in ports of call, where practicable, a medicine chest and medical guide, and access to radio or satellite medical advice.

Shipowners' liability (Reg 4.2). The shipowner bears the cost of sickness and injury occurring in service, and - since the 2014 amendments - must hold financial security for contractual claims arising from death or long-term disability.

Health and safety (Reg 4.3). Occupational safety and health policies and programmes, risk assessment and accident reporting, and - Standard A4.3.2 - a ship's safety committee where there are five or more seafarers. The 2016 amendments brought harassment and bullying expressly into the guidance.

Welfare and social security (Regs 4.4 and 4.5). Access to shore-based welfare facilities, and social security protection which, on ratification, must cover at least three of the nine branches listed in Standard A4.5.

blocks.h: 5. Flag State enforcement - certification and inspection

blocks.p: Title 5 is what makes the MLC enforceable rather than aspirational, and limb (b) cannot be answered without it.

The flag State certifies. Standard A5.1.3.1 - the maritime labour certificate is issued by the competent authority, or by a recognized organization duly authorized under Reg 5.1.2, for a period not exceeding five years, and is subject under A5.1.3.2 to an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates. It is accompanied by the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I, drawn by the competent authority, listing the national requirements; and Part II, drawn by the shipowner, setting out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance between inspections.

Appendix A5-I lists the working and living conditions that must be inspected and approved before certification. At this sitting there are sixteen - minimum age, medical certification, qualifications, seafarers' employment agreements, use of licensed recruitment services, hours of work or rest, manning levels, accommodation, on-board recreational facilities, food and catering, health and safety and accident prevention, on-board medical care, on-board complaint procedures, payment of wages, financial security for repatriation and financial security relating to shipowners' liability. The last two were added by the 2014 amendments, which is why the list is sixteen and not the original fourteen. Beyond certification, Reg 5.1.4 requires a system of inspection and enforcement, Reg 5.1.5 requires on-board complaint procedures with safeguards against victimization and the right to complain directly to the master and to external authorities, and Reg 5.1.6 requires an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty.

blocks.h: 6. Port State control and the labour-supplying State

blocks.p: Under Regulation 5.2.1 an authorized officer in a port of another Member may inspect. The certificate and DMLC are accepted as prima facie evidence of compliance, and the inspection normally stops there. Standard A5.2.1.1 gives four triggers for a more detailed inspection:

ul: the required documents are not produced or maintained, are falsely maintained, lack the required information or are otherwise invalid;
there are clear grounds for believing that working and living conditions do not conform to the Convention;
there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship has changed flag to avoid compliance; or
there is a complaint alleging that specific conditions do not conform.

blocks.p: Appendix A5-III sets out the sixteen general areas open to such a detailed inspection - the same list as Appendix A5-I. Where conditions are clearly hazardous to safety, health or security, or the breach is serious or repeated, the ship may be detained until deficiencies are rectified. Article V.7 supplies the principle that makes this work commercially: ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified must not receive more favourable treatment than those of a ratifying State. Two further limbs complete the architecture - Reg 5.2.2, which requires onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedures, and Reg 5.3, which places responsibilities on labour-supplying States such as India for recruitment, placement and social protection of their seafarers.
The Convention's weaknesses are structural rather than textual, and limb (b) is asking you to name them.

ul: Flag State capacity and delegation. Certification is almost universally delegated to recognized organizations under Reg 5.1.2, and the recognized organization is paid by the shipowner it inspects. Administrations with large registers and small staffs rely on that delegation entirely, so the quality of enforcement varies with the register rather than with the Convention.

Documentary compliance. Because the certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence, a ship whose paperwork is in order will normally pass. The gap between a compliant file and a compliant ship is the central practical limitation.

Hours-of-rest records. The single most reported area of non-compliance, and structurally so: the record is generated by the person whose hours it records, under commercial pressure, on a ship manned to the minimum safe manning document. Port turnarounds, inspections and drills are absorbed by the crew and disappear from the record.

Uneven national implementation. Article VI.3 substantial equivalence and the non-mandatory status of Part B mean two ratifying States may impose materially different requirements. Seafarers of the same rank on the same trade can hold quite different entitlements.

The limits of port State control. An MLC inspection competes with SOLAS and MARPOL priorities during a short port stay; assessing wages, contracts and rest hours is a different skill from assessing equipment; and risk-based targeting under the regional memoranda means some ships are rarely inspected.

Who actually bears the sanction. Enforcement acts on the ship, through detention and delay. It does not reach the beneficial owner directly, and single-ship companies and layered ownership limit what a seafarer can recover. The 2014 financial security amendments were a direct response to exactly this problem in abandonment cases.

Under-use of complaint procedures. Reg 5.1.5 gives the right and forbids victimization, but seafarers on short contracts in a competitive market fear blacklisting, so complaints are made late, ashore, or not at all.

Social security. Reg 4.5 is the weakest Title in practice: only three of nine branches are required at ratification, and portability between flag, nationality and manning-agent jurisdictions remains unresolved.

External shocks. The COVID-19 crew change crisis demonstrated the ceiling: when States closed borders, seafarers served far beyond the repatriation limits and neither flag nor port States could give effect to Reg 2.5, notwithstanding repeated ILO and IMO appeals.

blocks.p: The marks are 8 + 8, and the two limbs are very different tasks. Limb (a) is coverage: the examiner has named five areas - employment contracts, working hours, accommodation, health and safety, medical care and welfare - and expects each to be reached. Route steps 2, 3 and 4 walk the Titles in order so that none is missed, which is the commonest way marks are lost here.

Limb (b) is evaluation, and it is the harder half. It names three targets - flag State jurisdiction, port State control, and non-compliance by shipowners and operators - so an answer that merely describes Title 5 has answered the wrong question. Steps 5 and 6 establish the machinery briefly because you cannot criticise what you have not described; step 7 is where the marks are.

blocks.h: The temporal boundary - and why it decides this answer

blocks.p: This question is dated. At the March 2024 sitting the Convention is in force as amended in 2014, 2016 and 2018. The 2022 amendments, approved at the 110th Session of the International Labour Conference in June 2022, entered into force afterwards. Almost every currently available MLC summary, training package and website describes the 2022 provisions as live, because today they are - but they were not at this sitting.
What that excludes from a March 2024 answer, established by direct comparison of the two ILO consolidated texts:

ul: Social connectivity, including internet access, as a recreational facility under Standard A3.1. The phrase appears only in the 2022 consolidation.
Appropriately-sized personal protective equipment, and the accompanying statement that engineering and design controls take precedence over PPE, under Standard A4.3. Only in the 2022 consolidation.
Investigation, recording and annual reporting of all seafarer deaths to the Director-General of the ILO for publication in a global register, under Standard A4.3.5. Only in the 2022 consolidation.
The requirement that the financial security certificate name the registered owner where different from the shipowner. Only in the 2022 consolidation.

blocks.p: What is safely in at this sitting, and equally checked: financial security for abandonment and for death or long-term disability (2014); harassment and bullying (2016); continued wages during captivity from piracy or armed robbery (2018). The visible consequence is that Appendix A5-I lists sixteen items, not the original fourteen - the two extra being the financial security items added in 2014.

ul: Writing limb (b) as a second description of Title 5. The examiner asked for challenges and limitations.
Saying the MLC is an IMO convention. It is an ILO convention.
Treating Part B Guidelines as mandatory. Article VI - Part A Standards bind; Part B must be given due consideration.
Giving only one of the two hours regimes. A Member fixes either maximum work or minimum rest, and you should give both sets of figures.
Confusing DMLC Part I (competent authority, national requirements) with Part II (shipowner, measures for ongoing compliance).
Forgetting Regulation 5.3, labour-supplying responsibilities - which is the limb that matters most to an Indian candidate.
Importing the 2022 amendments. See above.
The five named areas in limb (a). They are a checklist. Tick every one.

Accommodation applies by build date. Standard A3.1 construction requirements bite only on ships built on or after entry into force for that Member - a point candidates almost never make and which distinguishes a read answer from a remembered one.
"Less than twelve months". Standard A2.5.2(b) says less than, not "up to". The eleven-month contract exists for this reason.
Prima facie evidence. The certificate is not conclusive. Naming the four triggers at Standard A5.2.1.1 is what earns the port State marks.
No more favourable treatment (Article V.7) - the MLC has its own version, and it is what stops a non-ratifying flag being a commercial advantage.
Three of nine branches of social security. An exact number in the weakest Title.
"What documents prove MLC compliance, and who issues each?" - the maritime labour certificate and the DMLC; Part I by the competent authority, Part II by the shipowner.
"How long is the certificate valid and what happens in between?" - not exceeding five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates.
"State the hours of rest limits." - ten hours in any 24 and 77 in any seven days; or, on the hours-of-work basis, 14 in any 24 and 72 in any seven days.
"A seafarer has been on board thirteen months. What is wrong?" - Standard A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period before repatriation entitlement to be less than twelve months.
"Your ship is abandoned in a foreign port. What protects the crew?" - the financial security for abandonment under Standard A2.5.2, certificate carried on board.
"When can a PSCO go beyond checking the certificate?" - the four triggers at Standard A5.2.1.1.
"Why is a safety committee required on your ship?" - Standard A4.3.2, five or more seafarers.

blocks.p: The five Titles are the spine and they run in the order a seafarer experiences them: get on board (Title 1), terms of service (Title 2), live on board (Title 3), stay well (Title 4), who checks (Title 5). Route steps 2 to 4 are Titles 1 to 4; steps 5 to 7 are Title 5 and its shortfalls.

For limb (b), hold four failure points: who inspects (delegated, and paid by the inspected), what is inspected (paper, prima facie), who records (the seafarer records their own hours), and who pays (the ship is detained, the owner is remote).

ul: Articles IV, V.7, VI - rights; no more favourable treatment; Parts A and B and substantial equivalence.
Std A1.1 minimum age 16, night work under 18. Std A1.2.7 medical certificate two years, one year under 18, colour vision six years.
Std A2.1 the employment agreement. Std A2.3.5 14/72 or 10/77. Std A2.5.1-2 repatriation and less than twelve months. Reg 2.2, 2.4, 2.7 wages, leave, manning.

questions.understand_first: The MLC is an ILO convention, not an IMO one, and that shapes everything about it. It regulates the EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP rather than the ship, which is why its enforcement machinery had to be borrowed from the IMO world - certification, port State control, no more favourable treatment - and bolted onto a labour instrument. Limb (a) is a coverage test across the five Titles; limb (b) asks you to explain why an instrument with that much machinery still leaves seafarers abandoned, overworked and unpaid. The honest answer to limb (b) is that the enforcement is documentary, the inspector is often paid by the inspected, and the seafarer writes their own hours record. One warning that decides this answer: the 2022 amendments were NOT in force at this sitting, and nearly every current source will tell you they were.
questions.memory_cue: The five Titles run in the order a seafarer meets them: GET ON BOARD, TERMS, LIVE, WELL, CHECK (2, 3, 4, 5). Then limb (b) has four failure points to attack in route step 7: INSPECT, PAPER, RECORD, PAY (7).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the Convention is and how it is built. 2 (a) Minimum requirements and the employment agreement. 3 (a) Hours, wages, leave, repatriation, manning. 4 (a) Accommodation, catering, health, welfare, social security. 5 (b) Flag State certification and inspection. 6 (b) Port State control and the labour-supplying State. 7 (b) Challenges and limitations.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2-4 are the five areas the examiner named; step 7 is where limb (b) scores.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between Part A and Part B of the MLC Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article VI - Part A contains Standards and is mandatory. Part B contains Guidelines which are not mandatory, but Members must give them due consideration. Article VI.3 also permits substantial equivalence, allowing a Member to implement a Part A Standard differently provided it is substantially equivalent in achieving the general object and purpose.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating Part B as binding is the most common structural error on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the MLC hours of work and hours of rest limits.
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A2.3.5 - a Member fixes either maximum hours of work, not exceeding 14 in any 24-hour period and 72 in any seven-day period; or minimum hours of rest, not less than ten in any 24-hour period and 77 in any seven-day period. Rest may be in no more than two periods, one of at least six hours, with no more than fourteen hours between them.
retrieval_cards.why: Both regimes are needed - the Convention offers an either/or, not a single rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long is the maritime labour certificate valid, and what accompanies it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A5.1.3.1 - a period not exceeding five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates under A5.1.3.2. It is accompanied by the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance: Part I by the competent authority listing the national requirements, Part II by the shipowner setting out the measures for ongoing compliance between inspections.
retrieval_cards.why: The Part I / Part II split is asked in almost every oral on this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MLC provisions must NOT appear in an answer set in March 2024?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2022 amendments, which entered into force after this sitting: social connectivity including internet access as a recreational facility; appropriately-sized personal protective equipment and the precedence of engineering controls over PPE; investigation, recording and annual reporting of seafarer deaths to the ILO for a global register; and naming the registered owner on the financial security certificate. In force at this sitting are the 2014, 2016 and 2018 amendments only.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost every current MLC source describes the 2022 provisions as live.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When may a port State officer go beyond checking the certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A5.2.1.1 - where the required documents are not produced, not maintained, falsely maintained, lack required information or are otherwise invalid; where there are clear grounds for believing conditions do not conform; where there are reasonable grounds to believe the ship changed flag to avoid compliance; or where there is a complaint. Appendix A5-III lists the sixteen areas open to detailed inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: The certificate is prima facie evidence only, and these four triggers rebut it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does Appendix A5-I list sixteen items rather than fourteen?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2014 amendments added financial security for repatriation and financial security relating to shipowners' liability to the list of matters that must be inspected and approved before certification. Both were in force at the March 2024 sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise, dated detail that proves which amendment set the answer is written on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what circumstances is a seafarer entitled to repatriation, and after how long?
retrieval_cards.answer: Standard A2.5.1 - when the employment agreement expires while abroad; when it is terminated by the shipowner or by the seafarer for justified reasons; and when the seafarer is no longer able to carry out the duties or cannot be expected to. Standard A2.5.2(b) requires the maximum service period on board after which repatriation falls due to be less than twelve months.
retrieval_cards.why: "Less than twelve months" - not "up to" - is why eleven-month contracts exist.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are hours-of-rest records the most commonly falsified MLC requirement?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the record is generated by the person whose hours it records, on a ship manned to the minimum safe manning document, under commercial pressure. Port turnarounds, inspections and drills are absorbed by the crew and never reach the record. The structural conflict, not individual dishonesty, is the point.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the strongest single answer available for limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does Article V.7 provide and why does it matter commercially?
retrieval_cards.answer: Each Member must implement its responsibilities so that ships flying the flag of a State which has not ratified the Convention do not receive more favourable treatment than those of a ratifying State. It removes the commercial advantage of flagging out to a non-party.
retrieval_cards.why: The MLC has its own no-more-favourable-treatment clause, distinct from the IMO ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What responsibilities does Regulation 5.3 place on a labour-supplying State?
retrieval_cards.answer: Responsibilities for the recruitment, placement and social protection of its seafarers - implemented through Regulation 1.4 on recruitment and placement services and Regulation 4.5 on social security. It is the limb that applies to India as a major supplier of seafarers rather than as a flag State.
retrieval_cards.why: Routinely omitted, and the most directly relevant limb for an Indian candidate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give three exact MLC thresholds from Titles 1, 4 and 4 respectively.
retrieval_cards.answer: Minimum age 16 with night work prohibited under 18 (Standard A1.1); a ship's safety committee where there are five or more seafarers (Standard A4.3.2); and social security covering at least three of the nine branches at ratification (Standard A4.5.2).
retrieval_cards.why: Three exact numbers that are cheap to hold and rarely produced.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks with very different demands. Limb (a) is a coverage test across five named areas - employment contracts, working hours, accommodation, health and safety, medical care and welfare. Limb (b) is evaluative and names three targets - flag State jurisdiction, port State control and shipowner non-compliance - so describing Title 5 is not an answer to it.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks printed as 8 + 8. Limb (a) is best spent across the Titles in order so that none of the five named areas is dropped; limb (b) needs the machinery described briefly and the criticism at length.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can name Standards, not just describe conditions - A2.3.5 for hours, A5.1.3 for the certificate, A5.2.1.1 for the PSC triggers - and can then say why an instrument with that machinery still fails seafarers in practice.

Almost all currently available MLC material describes the 2022 provisions as operative.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW for the Convention itself. India is a Party and the Convention applies uniformly. Regulation 5.3 on labour-supplying responsibilities is the limb of most direct relevance to an Indian candidate and is included for that reason.
